entries.before: and this alteration can be supported by the authority of Homer himself, who not only demolishes but literally outrages the proverb. After picturing Agamemnon as the most valiant of men, he has Menelaus — who is only a fainthearted warrior — come unbidden to Agamemnon's banquet, the man who was feasting and offering sacrifices: so the worse comes to the better, not the better to the worse.
entries.after: 'and we can support this change with the authority of Homer himself, who not only demolishes the proverb but does outright violence to it. For after portraying Agamemnon as the bravest of men, he has Menelaus, who is only a fainthearted warrior, come uninvited to Agamemnon's banquet while Agamemnon is feasting and offering sacrifices. So in Homer it is not the better who comes uninvited to the worse, but the worse to the better.'
entries.assessor_fix: Light: show in plain order that Homer goes further and reverses the proverb: the weak Menelaus arrives uninvited at the brave Agamemnon's sacrificial feast, the worse coming to the better.

entries.before: This was the style of their conversation as they went along. Then Socrates dropped behind in a fit of abstraction and told Aristodemus, who was waiting for him, to go on ahead. When Aristodemus reached the house of Agathon, he found the doors wide open, and a comical thing happened. A servant coming out met him and led him at once into the banqueting hall, where the guests were already reclining, for the banquet was about to begin. 'Welcome, Aristodemus,' said Agathon as soon as he appeared. 'You are just in time to sup with us. If you come on any other matter, put it off and make one of us — I was looking for you yesterday and meant to have asked you, if I could have found you. But what have you done with Socrates?'
entries.after: This was the style of their conversation as they went along. Then Socrates, lost in thought, dropped behind and told Aristodemus, who had stopped to wait for him, to go on ahead. When Aristodemus reached Agathon's house, he found the doors wide open, and a comical thing happened. A servant coming out met him and led him straight into the dining hall, where the guests were reclining on their couches, for the banquet was about to begin. 'Welcome, Aristodemus,' said Agathon as soon as he appeared. 'You're just in time to have supper with us. If you've come about anything else, put it off and join us. I was looking for you yesterday — I meant to invite you, if only I'd been able to find you. But what have you done with Socrates?'
entries.assessor_fix: Light: everyday wording for Socrates lost in thought, joining the dinner and 'I meant to invite you', keeping every beat of the comic arrival without Socrates.
entries.renderer_notes: 'On their couches' added so that 'reclining' is picturable (Greek diners lay on couches), which also prepares 1.30 and 1.36.

entries.before: I turned round, but Socrates was nowhere to be seen. So I had to explain that he had been with me only a moment before, and that I had come by his invitation to the supper.

entries.renderer_notes: 'Aristodemus said' tag added after the first clause, parallel to 1.14. 'Said' rather than 'told me', so that 'me' in the next sentence can only be Aristodemus.

entries.before: The servant then assisted him to wash, and he lay down. Presently another servant came in and reported that our friend Socrates had retired into the portico of the neighboring house. 'There he is fixed,' the servant said, 'and when I call to him he will not stir.'
entries.after: The servant then helped him wash, and he took his place, reclining at the table. Soon another servant came in and reported that our friend Socrates had withdrawn into the porch of the house next door. 'He's standing there, rooted to the spot,' the servant said, 'and when I call him, he won't move.'
entries.assessor_fix: Light: plain wording for washing, reclining at table, Socrates withdrawing into the neighbour's porch and standing motionless, deaf to the servant's calls.
entries.renderer_notes: 'Portico' becomes 'porch' here and in 1.33, where Agathon refers back to it.

entries.before: 'Well, if you think so, I will leave him,' said Agathon. And then, turning to the servants, he added, 'Let us have supper without waiting for him. Serve up whatever you please, for there is no one to give you orders; up until now I have never left you to yourselves, but on this occasion imagine that you are our hosts, and that I and the company are your guests. Treat us well, and then we shall commend you.' After this, supper was served, but still no Socrates. During the meal Agathon several times expressed a wish to send for him, but Aristodemus objected. At last, when the feast was about half over — for the fit, as usual, was not of long duration — Socrates entered. Agathon, who was reclining alone at the end of the table, begged him to take the place next to him. ''I may touch you,' he said, 'and have the benefit of that wise thought which came into your mind in the portico, and is now in your possession — for I am certain that you would not have come away until you had found what you sought.''
entries.after: 'Well, if you think so, I'll leave him alone,' said Agathon. Then, turning to the servants, he added, 'Let's have supper without waiting for him. Serve whatever you like, since there's no one to give you orders — I've never left you to yourselves before. But this time, imagine that you are our hosts, and that I and the company are your guests. Treat us well, and we'll praise you for it.' After this, supper was served, but still there was no Socrates. During the meal Agathon said several times that he wanted to send for him, but Aristodemus objected. At last, when the feast was about half over — for his trance, as usual, did not last long — Socrates came in. Agathon, who was reclining alone at the end of the table, begged him to take the place next to him, 'so that I can touch you,' he said, 'and get the benefit of that wise thought that came to you in the porch and is now yours. For I'm certain you wouldn't have come away until you had found what you were looking for.'
entries.assessor_fix: Light: restore the purpose link (sit by me so that I can touch you and share that wise thought), fix the doubled quotation marks and lighten the stiff narration, keeping Agathon's teasing.
entries.renderer_notes: Purpose link restored ('so that I can touch you'), following Jowett's own 'that I may touch you'. The doubled quotation marks are removed and 'the fit' becomes 'his trance'.

entries.before: 'How I wish,' said Socrates, taking his place as he was desired, 'that wisdom could be infused by touch, out of the fuller into the emptier man, as water runs through wool out of a fuller cup into an emptier one. If that were so, how greatly should I value the privilege of reclining at your side! For you would have filled me full with a stream of wisdom plenteous and fair — whereas my own is of a very mean and questionable sort, no better than a dream. But yours is bright and full of promise, and was manifested forth in all the splendor of youth the day before yesterday, in the presence of more than thirty thousand Greeks.'
entries.after: 'How I wish,' said Socrates, taking his place as he had been asked, 'that wisdom could flow by touch from the fuller man into the emptier, the way water creeps along a thread of wool from a fuller cup into an emptier one. If that were so, how highly I would value the privilege of reclining at your side! For you would fill me to the brim with a rich and beautiful stream of wisdom, whereas my own is a very poor and questionable sort, no better than a dream. But yours is bright and full of promise. The day before yesterday, in the theater, it shone out in all the splendor of youth before more than thirty thousand Greeks.'
entries.assessor_fix: Substantive: present-day wording that keeps Socrates' irony and every image, makes the wool-thread siphon picturable, and replaces 'mean', 'plenteous' and 'manifested forth'.
entries.renderer_notes: The wool image is made picturable as water creeping along a thread of wool from cup to cup. 'In the theater' is added so that listeners connect this with Agathon's prize (1.5, 1.13). 'Hellenes' is kept as 'Greeks', as in the accepted modern-en; change it back if the reviewer wants Jowett's form of the name.

entries.before: 'You are mocking me, Socrates,' said Agathon, 'and before long you and I will have to determine who bears off the palm of wisdom — of this Dionysus shall be the judge. But at present you are better occupied with supper.'
entries.after: 'You're mocking me, Socrates,' said Agathon. 'Before long, you and I will have to settle which of us carries off the prize for wisdom, and Dionysus, god of wine and the theater, will be our judge. But for now, you'd better get on with your supper.'
entries.assessor_fix: Light: everyday idiom for the coming wisdom contest, a few words placing Dionysus as god of wine and the theatre, and a plain 'for now, eat'.
entries.renderer_notes: Dionysus is glossed in five words. 'Bears off the palm' becomes 'carries off the prize'.

entries.before: Socrates took his place on the couch, and supped with the rest. Then libations were offered, and after a hymn had been sung to the god, and the usual ceremonies completed, they were about to commence drinking when Pausanias said, 'And now, my friends, how can we drink with the least injury to ourselves? I can assure you that I feel severely the effects of yesterday's potations, and must have time to recover; and I suspect that most of you are in the same predicament, for you were of the party yesterday. Consider, then: how can the drinking be made easiest?'
entries.after: Socrates took his place on the couch and ate supper with the others. Then they poured out offerings of wine to the gods, sang a hymn to the god, and went through the other customary rites. They were about to start drinking when Pausanias said, 'Now, my friends, how can we drink with the least harm to ourselves? I can tell you that I'm still suffering badly from yesterday's drinking and need time to recover — and I suspect most of you are in the same state, since you were at the party yesterday too. So think it over: how can we make the drinking as easy as possible?'
entries.assessor_fix: Light: plain narration of the meal, the wine-offerings to the gods and the hymn, and Pausanias's hangover joke in everyday words.
entries.renderer_notes: 'Libations' is rendered as offerings of wine poured for the gods. Jowett's singular 'the god' for the hymn is kept.

entries.before: 'Then,' said Eryximachus, 'the weak heads like myself, Aristodemus, Phaedrus, and others who never can drink, are fortunate in finding that the stronger ones are not in a drinking mood. I do not include Socrates, who is able either to drink or to abstain, and will not mind whichever we do. Well, as none of the company seem disposed to drink much, I may be forgiven for saying, as a physician, that drinking deep is a bad practice, which I never follow if I can help it, and certainly do not recommend to another — least of all to any one who still feels the effects of yesterday's carouse.'
entries.after: 'In that case,' said Eryximachus, 'those of us who cannot hold our wine — myself, Aristodemus, Phaedrus, and others who can never drink much — are fortunate to find that the strong drinkers are not in the mood for drinking. I do not count Socrates: he can drink or abstain equally well, and will not mind whichever we do. Well, since none of the company seems inclined to drink much, I may be forgiven for saying, as a physician, that heavy drinking is a bad practice. I never indulge in it if I can help it, and I certainly do not recommend it to anyone else — least of all to someone who is still feeling the effects of yesterday's excesses.'
entries.assessor_fix: Light: modern idiom for holding one's drink and heavy drinking, keeping the aside about Socrates and Eryximachus's doctorly pomposity.
entries.renderer_notes: 'Weak heads' becomes 'can't hold our wine', and 'carouse' becomes 'excesses', which keeps the doctor's pomposity. Jowett's parenthesis about Socrates becomes its own sentence.

entries.before: 'which I am about to speak, but that of Phaedrus. For often he says to me in an indignant tone: What a strange thing it is, Eryximachus, that whereas other gods have poems and hymns made in their honor, the great and glorious god Love has no encomiast among all the poets who are so many. There are the worthy sophists too — the excellent Prodicus, for example, who have descanted in prose on the virtues of Heracles and other heroes. And, what is still more extraordinary, I have met with a philosophical work in which the utility of salt has been made the theme of an eloquent discourse, and many other like things have had a like honor bestowed upon them. And only to think that there should have been such eager interest created about them, and yet that to this day no one has ever dared worthily to hymn Love's praises! So entirely has this great deity been neglected. Now in this Phaedrus seems to me quite right, and therefore I want to offer him a contribution. Also I think that at the present moment we who are here assembled cannot do better than honor the god Love. If you agree with me, there will be no lack of conversation, for I mean to propose that each of us in turn, going from left to right, shall make a speech in honor of Love — let him give us the best which he can; and Phaedrus, because he is sitting first on the left hand, and because he is the father of the thought, shall begin.'
entries.after: 'that I am about to speak, but Phaedrus's. For he often complains to me indignantly, "How strange it is, Eryximachus, that other gods have poems and hymns composed in their honor, while the great and glorious god Love has not a single poet to praise him, out of all the many poets there are. The worthy sophists too — professional teachers such as the excellent Prodicus — have written prose speeches praising the virtues of Heracles and other heroes. And what is even more extraordinary, I once came across a philosophical book in which the usefulness of salt was made the subject of an eloquent speech, and many other things like that have been honored in the same way. Just think: people have taken such an eager interest in things like these, and yet to this day no one has ever dared to sing Love's praises as he deserves! That is how completely this great god has been neglected." Now I think Phaedrus is quite right about this, and so I want to offer him a contribution. Besides, I think that at this moment we who are gathered here could do nothing better than honor the god Love. If you agree with me, there will be no shortage of conversation, because I propose that each of us in turn, going from left to right, should make a speech in honor of Love. Let each of us give the best speech he can; and Phaedrus should begin, because he is sitting first on the left, and because he is the father of the idea.'
entries.assessor_fix: Substantive: present-day English keeping every item (hymns to other gods, sophists like Prodicus praising Heracles in prose, the book praising salt), mark where Phaedrus's complaint ends, and keep the left-to-right speech proposal.
entries.renderer_notes: Phaedrus's complaint is marked with straight double quotation marks nested inside Eryximachus's single-quoted speech, so it clearly ends before 'Now I think Phaedrus is quite right'. 'Sophists' is glossed as professional teachers, and 'sophists ... have written' fixes Jowett's 'Prodicus ... who have' agreement.

entries.before: 'No one will vote against you, Eryximachus,' said Socrates. 'How can I oppose your motion, who profess to understand nothing but matters of love? Nor, I presume, will Agathon and Pausanias — and there can be no doubt of Aristophanes, whose whole concern is with Dionysus and Aphrodite. Nor will anyone disagree of those whom I see around me. The proposal, as I am aware, may seem rather hard on those of us whose place is last; but we shall be content if we hear some good speeches first. Let Phaedrus begin the praise of Love, and good luck to him.' All the company expressed their assent and desired him to do as Socrates bade him.
entries.after: 'No one will vote against you, Eryximachus,' said Socrates. 'How could I oppose your motion, when the only subject I claim to understand is love? Nor, I imagine, will Agathon and Pausanias; and there's certainly no doubt about Aristophanes, the comic poet, whose whole concern is with Dionysus and Aphrodite — that is, with wine and the theater, and with love. Nor will anyone else I see around me disagree. I'm aware that the proposal may seem rather hard on those of us whose turn comes last, but we'll be content if we hear some good speeches first. Let Phaedrus begin the praise of Love, and good luck to him.' All the company agreed, and urged Phaedrus to do as Socrates had said.
entries.assessor_fix: Substantive: present-day syntax for Socrates' support of the motion, keeping his claim to know only about love, a few words glossing Aristophanes' Dionysus-and-Aphrodite joke, and a plain closing line.
entries.renderer_notes: Jowett's closing 'him' is identified as Phaedrus, the person Socrates told to begin.

entries.before: And Acusilaus agrees with Hesiod. Thus numerous are the witnesses who acknowledge Love to be the eldest of the gods. And not only is he the eldest, he is also the source of the greatest benefits to us. For I know of no greater blessing to a young man who is beginning life than a virtuous lover, or to the lover than a beloved youth. For the principle which ought to guide men who would live nobly — that principle, I say, neither kindred, nor honor, nor wealth, nor any other motive is able to implant so well as love. What am I speaking of? Of the sense of honor and dishonor, without which neither states nor individuals ever do any good or great work. And I say that a lover who is caught doing any dishonorable act, or submitting through cowardice when any dishonor is done to him by another, will be more pained at being detected by his beloved than at being seen by his father, or by his companions, or by anyone else. The beloved too, when he is found in any disgraceful situation, has the same feeling about his lover. And if there were only some way of contriving that a state or an army should be made up of lovers and their loves, they would be the very best governors of their own city, abstaining from all dishonor and emulating one another in honor; and when fighting at each other's side, although a mere handful, they would overcome the world.
entries.after: And Acusilaus, an early prose writer on the origins of the gods, agrees with Hesiod. So there are many witnesses who acknowledge that Love is the eldest of the gods. And he is not only the eldest; he is also the source of the greatest benefits to us. For, Phaedrus said, I know of no greater blessing for a young man who is starting out in life than a virtuous lover — an older man who loves and courts him — and no greater blessing for the lover than a beloved youth. For there is a principle that ought to guide men who want to live nobly, and I say that neither family, nor public honors, nor wealth, nor any other motive can instill that principle as well as love can. What do I mean? The sense of honor and dishonor, without which neither states nor individuals ever do any good or great work. And I say that if a lover is caught doing something dishonorable, or letting someone else dishonor him because he is too cowardly to defend himself, he will be more pained to be seen by his beloved than by his father, his companions, or anyone else. The beloved, too, when he is caught in any disgraceful situation, feels the same way about his lover. So if only there were some way to form a state or an army made up of lovers and their beloveds, they would be the very best governors of their own city, holding back from everything dishonorable and competing with one another for honor. And fighting side by side, even a mere handful of them would overcome the world.

entries.before: Love will make men dare to die for their beloved — love alone; and women as well as men. Of this, Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, is a monument to all Greece; for she was willing to lay down her life on behalf of her husband, when no one else would, although he had both a father and a mother. But the tenderness of her love so far exceeded theirs that she made them seem to be strangers in blood to their own son, and in name only related to him. And so noble did this action of hers appear to the gods, as well as to men, that among the many who have done virtuously she is one of the very few to whom, in admiration of her noble action, they have granted the privilege of returning alive to earth; such exceeding honor is paid by the gods to the devotion and virtue of love. But Orpheus, the son of Oeagrus, the harper, they sent empty away, and presented him only with an apparition of her whom he sought — they would not give her up herself, because he showed no spirit; he was only a harp-player, and did not dare like Alcestis to die for love, but was contriving how he might enter Hades alive. Moreover, they afterwards caused him to suffer death at the hands of women, as the punishment of his cowardliness.
entries.after: Love, and love alone, will make men dare to die for their beloved — and women as well as men. Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, stands as proof of this before all Greece. Her husband could escape death only if someone would die in his place, and she was willing to lay down her life for him when no one else would, although he had a father and a mother. But her love was so much tenderer than theirs that she made them seem like strangers to their own son, as if they were not his own flesh and blood but related to him in name only. And her deed seemed so noble, to the gods as well as to men, that of the many who have done noble deeds, she is one of the very few to whom the gods, in admiration of what she did, have granted the privilege of coming back alive to earth from the dead. That is how highly the gods honor devotion and virtue in love. But when Orpheus the harper, the son of Oeagrus, went down to Hades for his dead wife, the gods sent him away empty-handed. They showed him only a phantom of the woman he had come for, and would not give her up herself, because he showed no spirit. He was only a harp-player, and did not dare, as Alcestis did, to die for love; instead, he schemed to find a way into Hades while still alive. What is more, the gods later had him put to death at the hands of women, as the punishment for his cowardice.

entries.before: Very different was the reward of the true love of Achilles toward his lover Patroclus — his lover and not his love (the notion that Patroclus was the beloved one is a foolish error into which Aeschylus has fallen, for Achilles was surely the fairer of the two, fairer also than all the other heroes; and, as Homer informs us, he was still beardless and younger by far). And greatly as the gods honor the virtue of love, still the return of love on the part of the beloved to the lover is more admired and valued and rewarded by them, for the lover is more divine, because he is inspired by God. Now Achilles was quite aware, for his mother had told him, that he might avoid death and return home, and live to a good old age, if he abstained from slaying Hector. Nevertheless he gave his life to avenge his friend, and dared to die — not only in his defense, but even after he was dead. For this the gods honored him even above Alcestis, and sent him to the Islands of the Blessed. These are my reasons for affirming that Love is the eldest and noblest and mightiest of the gods, and the chief author and giver of virtue in life, and of happiness after death.
entries.after: Very different was the reward Achilles received for his true love toward Patroclus, who was his lover and not his beloved — that is, Patroclus was the older man who loved him, and Achilles the younger man he loved. The idea that Patroclus was the beloved is a foolish mistake made by the tragic poet Aeschylus, for Achilles was surely the more beautiful of the two, and more beautiful than all the other heroes too; and, as Homer tells us, he was still beardless and much younger. The gods do greatly honor the virtue of love; but they admire, value, and reward it even more when the beloved returns the love of his lover, for the lover is more divine than the beloved, since he is inspired by a god. Now Achilles knew very well, because his mother had told him, that if he held back from killing Hector — the Trojan who had killed Patroclus — he could escape death, return home, and live to a ripe old age. Nevertheless he gave his life to avenge his friend: he dared not only to die for him, but to die after him, when Patroclus was already dead. That is why the gods honored him even above Alcestis, and sent him to the Islands of the Blessed, the paradise of heroes. These are my reasons for declaring that Love is the eldest, the noblest, and the mightiest of the gods, and the chief author and giver of virtue in life and of happiness after death.

entries.before: This, or something close to it, was Phaedrus's speech. Several other speeches followed that Aristodemus couldn't remember, but the next one he recounted was Pausanias's. Pausanias began: Phaedrus, I don't think the question has been framed correctly. We shouldn't be asked to praise Love in such an undiscriminating way. If there were only one Love, what you said would be fine — but since there are more Loves than one, we should have started by deciding which of them we are praising. Let me fix this oversight. First I'll tell you which Love deserves our praise, and then I'll try to hymn that praiseworthy one in a manner worthy of him. For we all know that Love is inseparable from Aphrodite, and if there were only one Aphrodite there would be only one Love — but since there are two goddesses, there must be two Loves. And am I not right that there are two goddesses? The elder, who has no mother, is called the heavenly Aphrodite — she is the daughter of Uranus. The younger, the daughter of Zeus and Dione, we call Common; and the Love who works alongside her is rightly named Common, just as the other Love is called Heavenly. All the gods deserve praise, but not without distinguishing their natures — so I must try to distinguish the characters of the two Loves. Now, actions vary in value according to how they are performed.

entries.before: Take, for example, what we are doing right now — drinking, singing, and talking. These actions are not in themselves either good or evil; they turn out one way or the other depending on how they are done. Done well, they are good; done badly, they are evil. In the same way, not every love is noble and worthy of praise — only the love that has a noble purpose. The Love who is the offspring of the Common Aphrodite is essentially common and makes no distinctions. It is the love the meaner sort of men feel, directed equally at women and at youths, and it is of the body rather than the soul. The most foolish beings are the objects of this love, which cares only about getting what it wants and never about achieving its end nobly, and so it does good and evil quite indiscriminately. The goddess who is his mother is far younger than the other, and she was born of the union of male and female, partaking of both. But the offspring of the Heavenly Aphrodite comes from a mother in whose birth the female had no part — she is from the male only. This is the love that is directed toward youths, and because the goddess is older, there is nothing of wantonness in her. Those inspired by this love turn to the male, delighting in whoever has the more valiant and intelligent nature; and anyone can recognize the pure enthusiasts by the very character of their attachments.

entries.before: For they love not boys, but intelligent beings whose reason is beginning to develop — around the age when their beards begin to grow. The love of young boys, however, ought to be forbidden by law, because their future is uncertain: they may turn out good or bad, in body or soul, and much noble enthusiasm may be wasted on them. In this matter the good are a law to themselves, but the coarser sort of lovers ought to be restrained by force — just as we try to restrain them from fixing their affections on freeborn women. These are the people who bring reproach upon love; and some have been led to deny the lawfulness of such attachments altogether because they see the impropriety and evil in them. But surely nothing done decorously and lawfully can justly be censured.

entries.before: And so the ill repute into which these attachments have fallen in some places must be attributed to the bad character of those who condemn them — that is, to the self-seeking of the rulers and the cowardice of the ruled. On the other hand, the indiscriminate honor given to them in other countries is owing to the mental laziness of those who hold that opinion. In our own country a far better principle prevails, though, as I said, it's a rather perplexing one. Consider: open loves are held to be more honorable than secret ones, and the love of the noblest and highest is especially honorable, even when the beloved is less beautiful than others. Consider too the enormous encouragement the whole world gives the lover: he is not thought to be doing anything dishonorable — if he succeeds he is praised, and if he fails he is blamed. And in pursuing his love, custom allows him to do many strange things that philosophy would bitterly condemn if they were done from any motive of profit, or desire for office, or power.

entries.before: He may pray, beg, supplicate, swear oaths, sleep on a mat at the door, and endure a servitude worse than any slave's. In any other situation his friends and enemies alike would step in to stop him; but here no friend will be ashamed of him or admonish him, and no enemy will accuse him of meanness or flattery. The actions of a lover have a grace that ennobles them, and custom has decided they are highly commendable and bring no loss of character. And strangest of all, he alone may swear and forswear himself — so people say — and the gods will forgive his transgression, for there is no such thing as a lover's oath. Such is the complete liberty that gods and men have allowed the lover, according to the custom that prevails in our part of the world. From this point of view a man could fairly argue that in Athens to love and to be loved is considered a most honorable thing. But then again — when fathers forbid their sons to speak with their lovers and place them under a tutor whose job is to prevent any such thing, and when their companions and peers taunt them for anything of the sort they observe, and their elders refuse to silence these reproaches or rebuke them — anyone reflecting on all this would, on the contrary, conclude that we hold these practices to be utterly disgraceful.
entries.after: He may pray, beg, plead, swear oaths, sleep on a mat at the door, and endure a servitude worse than any slave's. In any other situation his friends and enemies alike would step in to stop him; but here no friend will be ashamed of him or admonish him, and no enemy will accuse him of servility or flattery. The actions of a lover have a grace that ennobles them, and custom has decided they are highly commendable and bring no loss of character. And strangest of all, he alone may swear an oath and break it — so people say — and the gods will forgive his transgression, for there is no such thing as a lover's oath. Such is the complete liberty that gods and men have allowed the lover, according to the custom that prevails in our part of the world. From this point of view a man could fairly argue that in Athens to love and to be loved is considered a most honorable thing. But then consider the other side. entries.before: But as I was saying at the start, the truth, I think, is this: whether such practices are honorable or dishonorable is not a simple question. They are honorable to whoever pursues them honorably, and dishonorable to whoever pursues them dishonorably. There is dishonor in yielding to the bad, or yielding in a bad way; but there is honor in yielding to the good, or yielding in an honorable way. Evil is the vulgar lover, who loves the body rather than the soul — he isn't even stable, because he loves something that is itself unstable, so when the bloom of youth he desired is gone, he takes wing and flies away, breaking all his words and promises. But the love of a noble disposition lasts a lifetime, for it becomes one with what is everlasting. The custom of our country would have both lover and beloved thoroughly tested — have us yield to the one sort of lover and avoid the other, and therefore it encourages some to pursue and others to flee, testing both the lover and the beloved in contests and trials until it becomes clear which class each of them belongs to.
entries.after: But as I was saying at the start, the truth, I think, is this: whether such practices are honorable or dishonorable is not a simple question. They are honorable to whoever pursues them honorably, and dishonorable to whoever pursues them dishonorably. There is dishonor in yielding — that is, in a beloved's granting physical favors — to a bad lover, or in yielding in a bad way; but there is honor in yielding to a good lover, or in yielding in an honorable way. And the bad lover is the common lover, inspired by the Common Love, who loves the body rather than the soul; for he is not even stable, since he loves something that is itself unstable. So when the bloom of youth he desired is over, he takes wing and flies away, despite all his words and promises. But the man who loves a noble character stays for life, because his love becomes one with what is everlasting. The custom of our country wants both kinds of lover to be tested well and truly, and wants the beloved to yield to the one sort and avoid the other. That is why it encourages lovers to pursue and the beloved to flee: it tests both lover and beloved in contests and trials, until each of them shows which of the two kinds he belongs to.

entries.before: Eryximachus spoke as follows: 'Since Pausanias made a fair beginning but a lame ending, I must try to supply his deficiency. I think he has rightly distinguished two kinds of love. But my art informs me further that this double love is not merely an affection of the human soul toward the fair, or toward anything else, but is to be found in the bodies of all animals and in the productions of the earth — and, I may say, in all that is. Such is the conclusion I seem to have gathered from my own art of medicine, from which I learn how great and wonderful and universal is the deity of love, whose empire extends over all things, divine as well as human. And I will begin from medicine, that I may do honor to my art. In the human body there are these two kinds of love, which are confessedly different and unlike, and being unlike, they have loves and desires which are unlike. The desire of the healthy is one, and the desire of the diseased is another. And as Pausanias was just now saying that to indulge good men is honorable and bad men dishonorable, so too in the body the good and healthy elements are to be indulged, and the bad elements and the elements of disease are not to be indulged, but discouraged.'
entries.after: Eryximachus spoke as follows: 'Since Pausanias made a fine beginning but a lame ending, I must try to supply what he left out. I think he was right to distinguish two kinds of love. But my own art, medicine, informs me further that this double love is not merely a feeling in human souls, directed toward beautiful people or toward anything else. It is also found in the bodies of all animals, in all that grows from the earth, and, I may say, in everything that exists. That is the conclusion I seem to have drawn from my own art of medicine, which teaches me how great and wonderful and universal a god Love is: his empire extends over all things, divine as well as human. And I will begin with medicine, to honor my own art. The human body contains these two kinds of love. Everyone agrees that they are different and unlike, and because they are unlike, what they love and desire is unlike too: what is healthy desires one thing, and what is diseased desires another. Pausanias said a moment ago that it is honorable to gratify good men — to yield to their love — and dishonorable to gratify bad ones. In the same way, in the body the good and healthy elements should be gratified, while the bad elements, the elements of disease, should not be gratified but discouraged.
entries.assessor_fix: Substantive: present-day sentences that keep Eryximachus's systematic, slightly pompous tone and every step (the double love reaches beyond the soul to all bodies and nature; healthy vs diseased desire), make 'indulge' clear, and keep the speech's quotation open until 4.5.
entries.renderer_notes: Opens Eryximachus's speech with a single quote and leaves it open. There is no mark at the end of 4.0-4.4, and the quote closes at the end of 4.5, following the house pattern for multi-paragraph speeches (6.9 to 6.10). 'Indulge' becomes 'gratify', glossed with 'to yield to their love' to tie it to Pausanias's term in chapter 3. The same verb is used in 4.3 for Jowett's 'accepting'. Jowett attaches 'confessedly different and unlike' to the two kinds of love, and that attachment is kept. 'The fair' becomes 'beautiful people', and 'productions of the earth' becomes 'all that grows from the earth'.

entries.before: And this is what the physician has to do, and in this the art of medicine consists — for medicine may be regarded generally as the knowledge of the loves and desires of the body, and how to satisfy them or not. The best physician is he who is able to separate fair love from foul, or to convert one into the other; and he who knows how to eradicate and how to implant love, whichever is required, and can reconcile the most hostile elements in the constitution and make them loving friends, is a skillful practitioner. Now the most hostile are the most opposite, such as hot and cold, bitter and sweet, moist and dry, and the like. My ancestor Asclepius, knowing how to implant friendship and accord in these elements, was the creator of our art, as the poets here tell us and I believe them; and not only medicine in every branch, but also the arts of gymnastics and husbandry, are under his dominion. Anyone who pays the least attention to the subject will also perceive that in music there is the same reconciliation of opposites. I suppose this must have been the meaning of Heraclitus, although his words are not accurate; for he says that The One is united by disunion, like the harmony of the bow and the lyre. Now there is an absurdity in saying that harmony is discord, or is composed of elements which are still in a state of discord.
entries.after: 'This is what the physician has to do, and this is what the art of medicine consists of. For medicine can be regarded, broadly speaking, as the knowledge of the body's loves and desires, and of how to satisfy them or not. The best physician is the one who can separate the beautiful love from the ugly, or turn one into the other. And a physician who knows how to root out love and how to plant it, whichever is needed, and who can reconcile the most hostile elements in the body's constitution and make them loving friends, is a skillful practitioner. Now the most hostile elements are the most opposite ones, such as hot and cold, bitter and sweet, moist and dry, and the like. My ancestor Asclepius — we doctors trace our descent from him — knew how to plant friendship and agreement in these elements, and so he created our art. That is what our poet friends here tell us, and I believe them. And not only medicine in all its branches, but also the arts of physical training and farming, are under Love's dominion. Anyone who gives the subject the slightest attention will also see that music involves the same reconciling of opposites. I suppose that must have been what the philosopher Heraclitus meant, although he did not put it accurately. For he says that the One is united by disunion, like the harmony of the bow and the lyre, in which string and frame pull against each other and so hold together. Now it is absurd to say that harmony is discord, or that it is made up of elements that are still in a state of discord.
entries.assessor_fix: Substantive: plain modern wording with brief context for Asclepius and Heraclitus's bow-and-lyre image, and a clear referent for 'his dominion' (the god Love, whose 'empire' 4.0 describes), keeping the hot/cold, bitter/sweet pairs.

Jowett's spelling 'Heracleitus' is restored under 'keep proper names as Jowett has them'; the accepted text had 'Heraclitus'. entries.before: But what he probably meant was that harmony is composed of differing notes of higher or lower pitch which disagreed once, but are now reconciled by the art of music — for if the higher and lower notes still disagreed, there could be no harmony, clearly not. For harmony is a symphony, and symphony is an agreement; but an agreement of disagreements while they disagree there cannot be — you cannot harmonize that which disagrees. In like manner rhythm is compounded of elements short and long, once differing and now in accord; which accordance, as in the former instance medicine, so in all these other cases music implants, making love and unison grow up among them. And thus music too is concerned with the principles of love in their application to harmony and rhythm. Again, in the essential nature of harmony and rhythm there is no difficulty in discerning love which has not yet become double. But when you want to use them in actual life, either in the composition of songs or in the correct performance of airs or metres already composed (which latter is called education), then the difficulty begins, and the good artist is needed.
entries.after: 'But what he probably meant was this: harmony is made of differing notes, of higher and lower pitch, that once disagreed but have now been reconciled by the art of music. For if the higher and lower notes still disagreed, there could be no harmony — clearly not. After all, harmony is consonance, that is, notes sounding together; and consonance is an agreement. But there can be no agreement between things that disagree, as long as they still disagree: you cannot harmonize what disagrees. In the same way, rhythm is made up of short and long beats, which once differed but are now in accord. And just as medicine plants this agreement in the body, so music plants it in all these cases, making love and unison grow up among them. So music, too, is concerned with the principles of love, as they apply to harmony and rhythm. Again, if you look at harmony and rhythm in their essential nature, it is easy to make out love in them, and there love has not yet become double: it has not yet split into a good kind and a bad kind. But when you want to use them in actual life, either in composing songs or in correctly performing melodies and verses already composed — which is what we call education, since that is how the young are trained — then the difficulty begins, and a good artist is needed.

entries.before: The course of the seasons is also full of both these principles; and when, as I was saying, the elements of hot and cold, moist and dry, attain the harmonious love of one another and blend in temperance and harmony, they bring to men, animals, and plants health and plenty, and do them no harm. But the wanton love, getting the upper hand and affecting the seasons of the year, is very destructive and injurious, being the source of pestilence and bringing many other kinds of diseases on animals and plants; for hoarfrost, and hail, and blight spring from the excesses and disorders of these elements of love — which to know in relation to the revolutions of the heavenly bodies and the seasons of the year is termed astronomy. Furthermore, all sacrifices and the whole province of divination, which is the art of communion between gods and men — these, I say, are concerned only with the preservation of the good and the cure of the evil love. For all manner of impiety is likely to ensue if, instead of accepting and honoring and reverencing the harmonious love in all his actions, a man honors the other love, whether in his feelings toward gods or parents, toward the living or the dead. Wherefore the business of divination is to see to these loves and to heal them, and divination is the peacemaker of gods and men, working by a knowledge of the religious or irreligious tendencies which exist in human loves. Such is the great and mighty — or rather omnipotent — force of love in general.
entries.after: 'The course of the seasons, too, is full of both these principles. When, as I was saying, the elements of hot and cold, moist and dry, come to feel a harmonious love for one another and blend with moderation and harmony, they bring health and plenty to men, animals, and plants, and do them no harm. But when the unruly love gets the upper hand and takes hold of the seasons of the year, it does great damage and harm. It is the source of plagues, and it brings many other kinds of disease on animals and plants; for frost, hail, and blight all spring from the excesses and disorders of these elements of love. The study of these elements of love, as they relate to the movements of the heavenly bodies and to the seasons of the year, is called astronomy. Furthermore, all sacrifices, and the whole field of divination — the reading of signs from the gods, the art through which gods and men communicate — are concerned, I say, only with preserving the good love and curing the bad. For every kind of impiety is likely to follow if, instead of yielding to, honoring, and revering the harmonious love in everything he does, a man honors the other love, whether in his feelings toward gods or parents, toward the living or the dead. That is why the task of divination is to watch over these loves and heal them; and divination is the peacemaker between gods and men, working through its knowledge of the pious and impious tendencies in human loves. Such is the great and mighty — or rather, the all-powerful — force of love in general.
entries.assessor_fix: Substantive: plain sentences for the seasons (balanced love brings health and plenty, unruly love plague, frost and blight), for what 'astronomy' studies, and for divination tending and healing the two loves between gods and men.

entries.before: Aristophanes professed to open another vein of discourse; he had a mind to praise Love in a manner unlike that of either Pausanias or Eryximachus. 'Mankind,' he said, 'judging by their neglect of him, have never, as I think, at all understood the power of Love. For if they had understood him they would surely have built noble temples and altars, and offered solemn sacrifices in his honor — but this is not done, and most certainly ought to be done: since of all the gods he is the best friend of men, the helper and the healer of the ills which are the great impediment to the happiness of the race. I will try to describe his power to you, and you shall teach the rest of the world what I am teaching you. In the first place, let me treat of the nature of man and what has happened to it; for the original human nature was not like the present, but different. The sexes were not two, as they are now, but originally three in number: there was man, woman, and the union of the two, having a name corresponding to this double nature, which once had a real existence, but is now lost — and the word Androgynous is only preserved as a term of reproach. In the second place, the primeval man was round, his back and sides forming a circle; and he had four hands and four feet, one head with two faces looking opposite ways, set on a round neck and precisely alike; also four ears, two sets of privy members, and the remainder to correspond.'
entries.after: Aristophanes announced that he would take the discussion in a new direction: he meant to praise Love in a different way from either Pausanias or Eryximachus. 'Mankind,' he said, 'has never understood the power of Love at all, in my view — you can tell from the way people neglect him. If they had understood him, they would surely have built him noble temples and altars and offered solemn sacrifices in his honor. None of this is done, though it most certainly ought to be — for of all the gods, Love is the best friend of human beings: he is our helper, and the healer of the ills that are the greatest obstacle to the happiness of our race. I will try to explain his power to you, and you must pass on to the rest of the world what I am teaching you. First, let me explain human nature and what has happened to it, because our original nature was not the same as it is now, but different. Originally there were not two sexes, as there are now, but three: man, woman, and a union of the two. This third sex had a name to match its double nature. It once really existed but has now been lost, and its name, "Androgynous," meaning man-woman, survives only as an insult. Second, the original human beings, of all three kinds, were round, their backs and sides forming a circle. Each of them had four hands and four feet, and one head on a round neck, with two faces, exactly alike, looking in opposite directions. Each also had four ears, two sets of genitals, and everything else to match.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: say plainly that Aristophanes set out to praise Love in a different way; untangle 'have never, as I think, at all understood'; explain that 'androgynous' means man-woman and survives only as an insult; make clear 'the primeval man' means every original human being of all three kinds; plain words for the doubled genitals and 'everything else to match'.
entries.renderer_notes: Aristophanes' speech runs 5.0-5.7, so per the glossary each paragraph opens a single quote and only 5.7 closes it. 'The primeval man' made explicitly plural ('the original human beings, of all three kinds') so 5.1 can continue with 'they'. 'Androgynous' kept capitalized as Jowett has it, in nested double quotes, glossed as man-woman.

entries.before: He could walk upright as men now do, backwards or forwards as he pleased, and he could also roll over and over at a great pace, turning on his four hands and four feet, eight in all, like tumblers going over and over with their legs in the air — this was when he wanted to run fast. Now the sexes were three, and such as I have described them, because the sun, moon, and earth are three; and the man was originally the child of the sun, the woman of the earth, and the man-woman of the moon, which is made up of sun and earth, and they were all round and moved round and round like their parents. Terrible was their might and strength, and the thoughts of their hearts were great, and they made an attack upon the gods. Of them is told the tale of Otys and Ephialtes who, as Homer says, dared to scale heaven, and would have laid hands upon the gods. Doubt reigned in the celestial councils. Should they kill them and annihilate the race with thunderbolts, as they had done the giants? Then there would be an end of the sacrifices and worship which men offered to them. But on the other hand the gods could not suffer their insolence to be unrestrained. At last, after a good deal of reflection, Zeus discovered a way. He said: 'I think I have a plan which will humble their pride and improve their manners — men shall continue to exist, but I will cut them in two and then they will be diminished in strength and increased in numbers; this will have the advantage of making them more profitable to us.'
entries.after: 'They could walk upright, as people do now, backwards or forwards as they pleased. But they could also roll over and over at great speed, turning on their four hands and four feet, eight limbs in all, like acrobats turning cartwheels, going over and over with their legs in the air; that was how they ran when they wanted to go fast. There were three sexes, of the kinds I have described, because the sun, the moon, and the earth are three. The man was originally the child of the sun, the woman the child of the earth, and the man-woman the child of the moon, which shares in both sun and earth; and they were all round, and moved round and round, like their parents. Their strength and might were terrifying, their pride and ambition were enormous, and they launched an attack on the gods. They are the ones in the story of Otys and Ephialtes, the two brothers who, as Homer says, dared to climb up to heaven and would have laid hands on the gods. The gods met in council in heaven and could not decide what to do. If they killed them and wiped out the whole race with thunderbolts, as they had once done to the giants, there would be an end of the sacrifices and worship that humans offered them. But on the other hand, the gods could not let such arrogance go unchecked. At last, after a great deal of thought, Zeus found a way. He said: "I think I have a plan that will humble their pride and improve their manners. Humans will go on existing, but I will cut each of them in two. Then they will be weaker in strength and greater in number, which will also have the advantage of making them more profitable to us.

entries.renderer_notes: Zeus's speech is nested inside Aristophanes' speech, so it takes double quotes; it continues into 5.2, so neither quote closes here. 'Tumblers' rendered as acrobats turning cartwheels. The 'because' in the sun/moon/earth sentence is kept as Jowett's causal step.

entries.before: 'They shall walk upright on two legs, and if they continue insolent and will not be quiet, I will split them again and they shall hop about on a single leg.' He spoke and cut men in two, like a sorb-apple which is halved for pickling, or as you might divide an egg with a hair; and as he cut them one after another, he bade Apollo give the face and the half of the neck a turn, in order that the man might contemplate the section of himself — he would thus learn a lesson of humility. Apollo was also bidden to heal their wounds and compose their forms. So he gave a turn to the face, and pulled the skin from the sides all over that which in our language is called the belly, like the purses which draw in, and he made one mouth at the center, which he fastened in a knot (the same which is called the navel). He also moulded the breast and took out most of the wrinkles, much as a shoemaker might smooth leather upon a last; he left a few, however, in the region of the belly and navel, as a memorial of the primeval state. After the division, the two parts of man, each desiring his other half, came together and, throwing their arms about one another, entwined in mutual embraces, longing to grow into one; and they were on the point of dying from hunger and self-neglect, because they did not like to do anything apart. When one of the halves died and the other survived, the survivor sought another mate — man or woman as we call them — being the sections of entire men or women, and clung to that.
entries.after: '"They will walk upright on two legs. And if they are still arrogant and will not keep quiet, I will split them again, and they can hop about on one leg." With that, he cut the humans in two, the way a sorb-apple, a small fruit, is halved for pickling, or the way you might slice an egg with a hair. As he cut them, one after another, he told Apollo to twist each one's face and half its neck around toward the cut side, so that the person could look at where he had been cut and learn a lesson in humility. Apollo was also told to heal their wounds and reshape their bodies. So Apollo turned the face around, and pulled the skin in from the sides over what we call the belly, gathering it like a drawstring purse. He made a single opening in the middle and tied it off in a knot, the one we call the navel. He also shaped the chest and smoothed out most of the wrinkles, much as a shoemaker smooths leather over a last, the foot-shaped block he works on. But he left a few wrinkles around the belly and navel, as a reminder of our original state. Once they had been cut in two, each half longed for its other half, and the halves came together. They threw their arms around one another, entwined in each other's embrace, longing to grow back into one; and they were on the point of dying of hunger and self-neglect, because they did not want to do anything apart. And when one half died and the other survived, the survivor looked for another mate — a man or a woman, as we call them now, though each was really only half of a whole man or a whole woman — and clung to that one.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: keep every simile but make each intelligible in a few words (sorb-apple = a small fruit halved for pickling; a drawstring purse; a shoemaker's last = foot-shaped form); say Apollo turned each face toward its cut side so the person could see it; 'opening' for 'mouth'; 'reshape their bodies' for 'compose their forms'; untangle 'being the sections of entire men or women'.
entries.renderer_notes: Opens with both marks: the single quote continues Aristophanes' speech and the double quote continues Zeus's, which closes after 'one leg.' Each simile glossed in a few words (sorb-apple, drawstring purse, shoemaker's last). 'Mouth' rendered as 'opening'; 'compose their forms' as 'reshape their bodies'.

entries.before: They were being destroyed, when Zeus in pity of them invented a new plan: he turned the parts of generation round to the front, for this had not always been their position, and they sowed the seed no longer as hitherto like grasshoppers in the ground, but in one another. After this transposition the male generated in the female, in order that by the mutual embraces of man and woman they might breed, and the race might continue; or, if man came to man, they might be satisfied, and rest, and go their ways to the business of life — so ancient is the desire of one another which is implanted in us, reuniting our original nature, making one of two, and healing the state of man. Each of us, when separated, having one side only, like a flat fish, is but the indenture of a man, and he is always looking for his other half. Men who are a section of that double nature which was once called Androgynous are lovers of women; adulterers are generally of this breed, and also adulterous women who lust after men. The women who are a section of the original woman do not care for men, but have female attachments — the female companions are of this sort. But they who are a section of the male follow the male, and while they are young, being slices of the original man, they hang about men and embrace them, and they are themselves the best of boys and youths, because they have the most manly nature.
entries.after: 'They were dying out when Zeus took pity on them and came up with a new plan. He moved their genitals round to the front, where they had not always been. Until then they had sown their seed not in one another but in the ground, the way grasshoppers lay their eggs in the earth; from then on they sowed it in one another. After this change, the male reproduced in the female, so that when a man and a woman embraced they would have children, and the race would continue; or, if a man came together with a man, they would be satisfied, and could rest, and get on with the business of life. That is how ancient our inborn desire for one another is. It brings our original nature back together, making one out of two and healing the human condition. Each of us, once separated and left with only one side, like a flatfish, is only half of a human being, like one half of a token split in two that matches nothing but its partner; and each of us is always looking for his other half. Men who are halves of the double being once called Androgynous are lovers of women; most adulterers come from this stock, and so do adulterous women who lust after men. Women who are halves of an original woman do not care for men, but are drawn to women; women who take other women as lovers are of this kind. But those who are halves of an original male pursue males. While they are young, being slices of the original man, they hang around men and embrace them; and they are the best of boys and young men, because they have the most manly nature.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: replace 'indenture' (today a contract) with the image Jowett means, one half of a split token looking for its match; plain words for genitals and reproduction; make the insect image clear (creatures thought to breed in the earth); make clear 'the female companions' are women who love women; 'those who' for 'they who'.
entries.renderer_notes: 'Indenture' rendered as its meaning, one half of a split token that matches only its partner (the same image as the tallies in 5.6). 'The female companions' made explicit as women who take other women as lovers. Frank, plain terms for genitals and reproduction.

entries.before: Some indeed assert that they are shameless, but this is not true; for they do not act thus from any want of shame, but because they are valiant and manly, and have a manly countenance, and they embrace that which is like them. And these, when they grow up, become our statesmen — and these only — which is a great proof of the truth of what I am saying. When they reach manhood they are lovers of youth, and are not naturally inclined to marry or beget children; if they do so at all, it is only in obedience to the law, but they are satisfied if they may be allowed to live with one another unwedded. And such a nature is prone to love and ready to return love, always embracing that which is akin to him. And when one of them meets with his other half — the actual half of himself, whether he be a lover of youth or a lover of another sort — the pair are lost in an amazement of love and friendship and intimacy, and one will not be out of the other's sight, as I may say, even for a moment. These are the people who pass their whole lives together, yet they could not explain what they desire of one another. For the intense yearning which each of them has toward the other does not appear to be the desire of lover's intercourse, but of something else which the soul of either evidently desires and cannot tell, and of which she has only a dark and doubtful presentiment.
entries.after: 'Some people say that they are shameless, but that is not true. They do not behave this way from any lack of shame, but because they are brave and manly and have a manly look, and they embrace what is like themselves. And when they grow up, these are the men who become our statesmen, and they are the only ones who do, which is strong proof that what I am saying is true. As grown men they are lovers of youths — that is, they court younger men — and by nature they are not inclined to marry or have children. If they do so at all, it is only because law and custom require it; they are content to live with one another unmarried, if they are allowed to. A man of this nature is quick to love and ready to return love, always embracing what is akin to him. And when one of them meets his other half, the actual half of himself, whether he is a lover of youths or a lover of some other kind, the pair are lost in amazement, overcome by love and friendship and intimacy, and neither will let the other out of his sight even for a moment, so to speak. These are the people who spend their whole lives together, and yet they could not explain what they want from each other. For the intense longing each feels for the other does not seem to be a desire for sexual union, but for something else. The soul of each clearly desires something it cannot put into words, something it senses only darkly and doubtfully.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: say plainly that as grown men they take younger male partners rather than marry (what 'lovers of youth' means; today it could read as 'fond of youthfulness'); 'lack of shame'; 'have children'; end with a clear sentence that each soul longs for something it cannot put into words and only dimly senses.
entries.renderer_notes: 'Lovers of youth' glossed as courting younger men (the older lover courting the younger beloved). 'Lover's intercourse' rendered as sexual union. The last sentence is split so the soul's wordless, dimly sensed longing stands as a clear sentence of its own.

entries.before: Suppose Hephaestus, with his instruments, to come to the pair who are lying side by side, and to say to them: 'What do you people want of one another?' — they would be unable to explain. And suppose further, that when he saw their perplexity he said: 'Do you desire to be wholly one; always day and night to be in one another's company? For if this is what you desire, I am ready to melt you into one and let you grow together, so that being two you shall become one, and while you live you shall live a common life as if you were a single man, and after your death in the world below you shall still be one departed soul instead of two — I ask whether this is what you lovingly desire, and whether you are satisfied to attain this?' There is not a man of them who, when he heard the proposal, would deny or would not acknowledge that this meeting and melting into one another, this becoming one instead of two, was the very expression of his ancient need. And the reason is that human nature was originally one, and we were a whole, and the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love. There was a time, I say, when we were one; but now, because of the wickedness of mankind, God has dispersed us, as the Arcadians were dispersed into villages by the Lacedaemonians.
entries.after: 'Suppose Hephaestus, the blacksmith god, came with his tools to the pair as they lay side by side, and asked them, "What is it you people want from each other?" They would not be able to explain. And suppose further that, seeing how puzzled they were, he said: "Do you want to be wholly one, always together, day and night? Because if that is what you want, I am ready to melt you into one and let you grow together, so that the two of you will become one. As long as you live, you will share a single life, as if you were one person; and after you die, down in the world below, you will still be one departed soul instead of two. So I ask you: is this what your love desires, and would you be satisfied to have it?" Every one of them, on hearing this offer, would agree, and not one would deny, that this meeting and melting into one another, this becoming one instead of two, was the very expression of his age-old need. And the reason is that human nature was originally one and we were a whole, and the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love. There was a time, I say, when we were one; but now, because of the wickedness of humankind, the god has dispersed us, just as the Lacedaemonians, that is, the Spartans, dispersed the Arcadians into villages.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: 'Suppose Hephaestus, the blacksmith god, came with his tools...'; turn the double negative into a plain 'every one of them would agree that'; identify the Lacedaemonians as the Spartans who broke the Arcadians' city up into villages.

Jowett's 'God' rendered 'the god' (Plato's ho theos), since a capital-G God reads as monotheistic today; Jowett's bracketed 'compare Arist. Pol.' notes omitted.

entries.before: And if we are not obedient to the gods, there is a danger that we shall be split up again and go about in basso-relievo, like the profile figures with only half a nose which are sculptured on monuments, and that we shall be like tallies. Wherefore let us exhort all men to piety, that we may avoid evil, and obtain the good, of which Love is to us the lord and minister; and let no one oppose him — he is the enemy of the gods who opposes him. For if we are friends of the God and at peace with him we shall find our own true loves, which rarely happens in this world at present. I am serious, and therefore I must beg Eryximachus not to make fun of me or to find any allusion in what I am saying to Pausanias and Agathon, who, as I suspect, are both of the manly nature, and belong to the class which I have been describing. But my words have a wider application — they include men and women everywhere; and I believe that if our loves were perfectly accomplished, and each one returning to his primeval nature had his original true love, then our race would be happy. And if this would be best of all, the best in the next degree and under present circumstances must be the nearest approach to such a union; and that will be the attainment of a congenial love.
entries.after: 'And if we do not obey the gods, there is a danger that we will be split in two again and go about like the flat figures carved in profile on monuments, with only half a nose; and that we will be like tallies, those tokens split in two whose halves match only each other. So let us urge everyone to show reverence toward the gods, in order that we may avoid evil and obtain the good, which Love rules over and brings to us. And let no one oppose Love: whoever opposes him is an enemy of the gods. For if we are friends of the god and at peace with him, we will find the loves that are truly our own, which rarely happens in this world at present. I am being serious, so I must beg Eryximachus not to make fun of this, or to find in what I am saying any allusion to Pausanias and Agathon, who, I suspect, are both of the manly kind and belong to the class I have been describing. But my words apply more widely: they include men and women everywhere. entries.after: The speakers before me, instead of praising the god Love or revealing his nature, seem to have congratulated mankind on the benefits he bestows on them. But I would rather praise the god first, and then speak of his gifts; that is always the right way to praise anything. May I say, without irreverence or offense, that of all the blessed gods Love is the most blessed, because he is the most beautiful and the best? And he is the most beautiful, first of all because he is the youngest. He himself is the witness of his own youth, for he flees from Old Age — and Old Age is swift enough, swifter, truly, than most of us would like. Love hates Old Age and will not come near him; but youth and love live and move together, for, as the proverb says, like is drawn to like. Phaedrus said many things about Love that I agree with; but I cannot agree that Love is older than Iapetus and Kronos, the ancient Titans. Not so! I maintain that he is the youngest of the gods, and forever young. The ancient doings among the gods, those deeds of divine violence that the poet Hesiod and the philosopher-poet Parmenides told of, were, if the stories are true, the work of Necessity, the power of compulsion, and not of Love. Had Love been there in those days, there would have been no chaining or mutilating of gods, and no other violence, but peace and sweetness, as there is now in heaven, ever since Love began to reign. Love is young, and he is also tender. He deserves a poet like Homer to describe his tenderness, the way Homer says of Ate, the goddess of ruin, that she is a goddess and tender:

entries.after: Here is excellent proof of her tenderness: she walks not on what is hard, but on what is soft. Let me offer a similar proof of the tenderness of Love. He walks not on the earth, nor even on the skulls of men, which are not so very soft, but in the hearts and souls of both gods and men, which are the softest things of all: in them he walks and dwells and makes his home. Yet not in every soul without exception; for where there is hardness he departs, and where there is softness, there he dwells. And since he always nestles, with his feet and in every other way, in the softest of soft places, how can he be anything but the softest of all things? Truly, then, he is the tenderest as well as the youngest; and he is also supple in form. For if he were hard and unbending, he could not wrap himself around all things, or wind his way unnoticed into and out of every human soul. And proof of his suppleness and the fine proportions of his form is his grace, which everyone agrees belongs to Love in a special way; gracelessness and love are forever at war with each other. The beauty of his coloring is shown by his home among the flowers. For he does not live among beauties that have no bloom or are fading, whether of body or soul or anything else; but wherever there are flowers and scents, there he settles, and there he stays. About the beauty of the god I have said enough — and yet there is much more that I could say.

entries.before: Of his virtue I have now to speak: his greatest glory is that he can neither do nor suffer wrong to or from any god or any man; for he suffers not by force if he suffers — force comes not near him, neither when he acts does he act by force. For all men in all things serve him of their own free will, and where there is voluntary agreement, there, as the laws which are the lords of the city say, is justice. And not only is he just, but exceedingly temperate; for Temperance is the acknowledged ruler of the pleasures and desires, and no pleasure ever masters Love — he is their master and they are his servants; and if he conquers them he must be temperate indeed. As to courage, even the God of War is no match for him; he is the captive and Love is the lord, for love, the love of Aphrodite, masters him, as the tale runs; and the master is stronger than the servant. And if he conquers the bravest of all others, he must be himself the bravest. Of his courage and justice and temperance I have spoken; but I have yet to speak of his wisdom, and according to the measure of my ability I must try to do my best. In the first place he is a poet (and here, like Eryximachus, I magnify my art), and he is also the source of poesy in others — which he could not be if he were not himself a poet.
entries.after: Now I must speak of his virtue. His greatest glory is that he can neither do wrong to any god or any man, nor suffer wrong from any god or any man. The reason is that if anything is done to him, it is not done by force, since force never comes near him; and when he acts, he does not act by force. For everyone serves Love in everything of their own free will, and where there is willing agreement, there, as the laws that are the lords of the city declare, is justice. So he is just; and not only just, but supremely self-controlled. For self-control is acknowledged to be the ruler of the pleasures and desires, and no pleasure ever masters Love: he is their master, and they are his servants. And if he conquers them, he must be self-controlled indeed. As for courage, even Ares, the God of War, is no match for him. Ares is the captive and Love is the lord; for love, his love for Aphrodite, masters him, as the story goes; and the master is stronger than the servant. And if Love conquers the bravest of all the others, he himself must be the bravest. I have spoken of his courage and justice and self-control; but I have yet to speak of his wisdom, and I must try to do my best, as far as my ability allows. In the first place, he is a poet — and here, like Eryximachus, I am praising my own art — and he is also the source of poetry in others, which he could not be if he were not a poet himself.

entries.before: This is he who empties men of disaffection and fills them with affection, who makes them to meet together at banquets such as these; in sacrifices, feasts, dances, he is our lord — who sends courtesy and sends away discourtesy, who gives kindness ever and never gives unkindness; the friend of the good, the wonder of the wise, the amazement of the gods; desired by those who have no part in him, and precious to those who have the better part in him; parent of delicacy, luxury, desire, fondness, softness, grace; regardful of the good, regardless of the evil; in every word, work, wish, fear — savior, pilot, comrade, helper; glory of gods and men, leader best and brightest; in whose footsteps let every man follow, sweetly singing in his honor and joining in that sweet strain with which love charms the souls of gods and men. Such is the speech, Phaedrus, half-playful yet having a certain measure of seriousness, which, according to my ability, I dedicate to the god.
