entries.before: 'Why, my dear friend,' said Socrates, 'must not I or anyone be in a strait who has to speak after he has heard such a rich and varied discourse? I am especially struck with the beauty of the concluding words — who could listen to them without amazement? When I reflected on the immeasurable inferiority of my own powers, I was ready to run away for shame, if there had been a possibility of escape. For I was reminded of Gorgias, and at the end of his speech I fancied that Agathon was shaking at me the Gorginian or Gorgonian head of the great master of rhetoric, which was simply to turn me and my speech into stone, as Homer says, and strike me dumb. And then I perceived how foolish I had been in consenting to take my turn with you in praising love, and saying that I too was a master of the art, when I really had no conception how anything ought to be praised. For in my simplicity I imagined that the topics of praise should be true, and that, this being presupposed, out of the true the speaker was to choose the best and set them forth in the best manner. And I felt quite proud, thinking that I knew the nature of true praise, and should speak well. Whereas I now see that the intention was to attribute to Love every species of greatness and glory, whether really belonging to him or not, without regard to truth or falsehood — that was no matter; for the original proposal seems to have been not that each of you should really praise Love, but only that you should appear to praise him.
entries.after: 'Why, my dear friend,' said Socrates, 'wouldn't I, or anyone, be at a loss, having to speak after hearing such a rich and varied speech? I am especially struck by the beauty of the closing words — who could listen to them without amazement? When I thought how immeasurably inferior my own powers are, I was ready to run away in shame, if there had been any way to escape. For the speech reminded me of Gorgias, the famous orator; and at its end I imagined Agathon shaking at me the Gorginian — or should I say Gorgonian — head of that great master of rhetoric. Like the head of the monster Gorgon, it was meant simply to turn me and my speech to stone, as Homer says, and strike me dumb. And then I realized how foolish I had been to agree to take my turn with you in praising love, and to say that I too was a master of the art, when in fact I had no idea how anything ought to be praised. For in my simplicity I imagined that whatever is said in praise should be true; and that, with truth as the starting point, the speaker should choose the finest of these truths and set them out in the best way. And I felt quite proud, thinking that I knew the nature of true praise and would speak well. But now I see that the idea was to credit Love with every kind of greatness and glory, whether it really belonged to him or not, without regard to truth or falsehood — that did not matter. For the original proposal, it seems, was not that each of you should really praise Love, but only that you should appear to praise him.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: a plain question ('wouldn't anyone be at a loss...'); a few words so the pun works (Agathon's style echoes the orator Gorgias, and Socrates fears a Gorgon's head that turns listeners to stone); lay out his old view of praise in order: tell the truth, choose the finest truths, arrange them well; 'every kind of'.
entries.renderer_notes: Socrates' speech runs 6.9-6.10: the quote opens here and closes only at the end of 6.10. The Gorgias/Gorgon pun is kept with both of Jowett's adjectives, and Gorgias (the orator) and the Gorgon (the monster whose head turns people to stone) are each identified in a few words. Jowett's '(Odyssey)' note omitted. His view of praise is laid out in order: tell the truth, choose the finest truths, present them well.

entries.before: And so you attribute to Love every imaginable form of praise which can be gathered anywhere; and you say that "he is all this," and "the cause of all that," making him appear the fairest and best of all to those who know him not — for you cannot impose upon those who know him. And a noble and solemn hymn of praise have you rehearsed. But as I misunderstood the nature of the praise when I said that I would take my turn, I must beg to be absolved from the promise which I made in ignorance, and which (as Euripides would say) was a promise of the lips and not of the mind. Farewell then to such a strain — for I do not praise in that way; no, indeed, I cannot. But if you like to hear the truth about love, I am ready to speak in my own manner, though I will not make myself ridiculous by entering into any rivalry with you. Say then, Phaedrus, whether you would like to have the truth about love, spoken in any words and in any order which may happen to come into my mind at the time. Will that be agreeable to you?'
entries.after: 'And so you attribute to Love every imaginable form of praise that can be gathered from anywhere; and you say that "he is all this," and "the cause of all that," making him appear the most beautiful and best of all to people who do not know him — for you cannot fool those who do. And what a noble, solemn hymn of praise you have delivered! But since I misunderstood the nature of the praise when I said that I would take my turn, I must beg to be released from the promise I made in ignorance, which, as Euripides would say, was a promise of the lips and not of the mind. So goodbye to that style of praise, for I do not praise in that way — no, indeed, I cannot. But if you would like to hear the truth about love, I am ready to speak in my own manner, though I will not make myself ridiculous by entering into any rivalry with you. So tell me, Phaedrus, whether you would like to hear the truth about love, spoken in whatever words and in whatever order happen to come into my mind at the time. Would that suit you?'

entries.before: In the magnificent speech you just gave, dear Agathon, I think you were right to begin by describing Love's nature before discussing his works — that's an approach I very much approve of. And since you've spoken so eloquently about his nature, may I ask you one more thing: Is love the love of something, or of nothing? And here I must explain myself. I don't want you to say that love is the love of a father or the love of a mother — that would be ridiculous. But to answer as you would if I asked, is a father a father of something? To which you would find no difficulty in replying, of a son or daughter: and the answer would be right.
entries.after: 'In the magnificent speech you have just given, my dear Agathon, I think you were right to propose speaking first of the nature of Love and afterwards of his works — that is a way of beginning I very much approve of. And since you have spoken so eloquently of his nature, may I ask you something further: is love the love of something, or of nothing — does it always have an object? Here I must explain myself. I am not asking whose child Love is, as though he were the love of some father or mother; that would be a ridiculous question. I am asking the kind of thing I would be asking if I said: is a father the father of something? You would have no difficulty in replying that he is the father of a son or a daughter, and that answer would be right.'

entries.before: 'And yet,' added Socrates, 'if a man being strong desired to be strong, or being swift desired to be swift, or being healthy desired to be healthy, in that case he might be thought to desire something which he already has or is. I give the example in order that we may avoid misconception. For the possessors of these qualities, Agathon, must be supposed to have their respective advantages at the time, whether they choose or not — and who can desire that which he has? Therefore, when a person says, "I am well and wish to be well," or "I am rich and wish to be rich, and I desire simply to have what I have" — to him we shall reply: "You, my friend, having wealth and health and strength, want to have the continuance of them; for at this moment, whether you choose or no, you have them. And when you say, I desire that which I have and nothing else, is not your meaning that you want to have what you now have in the future?" He must agree with us — must he not?'
entries.after: 'And yet,' added Socrates, 'suppose a man who is strong desires to be strong, or a man who is swift desires to be swift, or a man who is healthy desires to be healthy. In that case he might be thought to desire something he already has, or already is. I give this example so that we do not fall into a misunderstanding. For we must suppose, Agathon, that people who possess these qualities have their advantages at the present moment, whether they like it or not; and who can desire what he already has? So when someone says, "I am well and wish to be well," or "I am rich and wish to be rich, and I desire simply to have what I have," we shall reply to him: "My friend, you have wealth and health and strength, and what you want is to go on having them; for at this moment, whether you like it or not, you have them. So when you say that you desire what you have and nothing else, don't you really mean that you want to have in the future what you have now?" He must agree with us — mustn't he?'
entries.assessor_fix: Recast in plain syntax: a strong man who says he wants to be strong seems to want what he has, but he has it now whether he likes it or not, so what he wants is to keep it in the future; keep all three examples, the imagined reply and the closing check.
entries.renderer_notes: Rendered as indirect speech, 'when you say that you desire what you have and nothing else', to avoid a third level of quotation marks. The question keeps 'must' so that Agathon's KEEP reply 'He must' (7.21) still fits.

entries.before: 'And now, taking my leave of you, I would rehearse a tale of love which I heard from Diotima of Mantineia, a woman wise in this and in many other kinds of knowledge, who in the days of old, when the Athenians offered sacrifice before the coming of the plague, delayed the disease ten years. She was my instructress in the art of love, and I shall repeat to you what she said to me, beginning with the admissions made by Agathon, which are nearly if not quite the same as those which I made to the wise woman when she questioned me. I think that this will be the easiest way, and I shall take both parts myself as well as I can. As you, Agathon, suggested, I must speak first of the being and nature of Love, and then of his works. First I said to her, in nearly the same words which he used to me, that Love was a mighty god, and likewise fair; and she proved to me, as I proved to him, that, by my own showing, Love was neither fair nor good. "What do you mean, Diotima," I said, "is love then evil and foul?" "Hush," she cried, "must that be foul which is not fair?" "Certainly," I said. "And is that which is not wise, ignorant? Do you not see that there is a mean between wisdom and ignorance?" "And what may that be?" I said.'
entries.after: 'And now I will leave you in peace, and tell a story about love that I heard from Diotima of Mantineia, a woman wise in this and in many other kinds of knowledge. Long ago, when the Athenians offered sacrifices before the plague came, she delayed the disease for ten years. She was my teacher in the art of love, and I shall repeat to you what she said to me. I will begin with the points Agathon admitted, which are nearly, if not quite, the same as those I admitted to the wise woman when she questioned me. I think this will be the easiest way, and I shall take both parts myself, hers and mine, as well as I can. As you suggested, Agathon, I must speak first of the being and nature of Love, and then of his works. First I said to her in nearly the same words that Agathon used to me: that Love was a mighty god, and beautiful as well. And she proved to me, just as I proved to him, that by my own argument Love was neither beautiful nor good. "What do you mean, Diotima?" I said. "Is love then bad and ugly?" "Hush," she cried. "Must whatever is not beautiful be ugly?" "Certainly," I said. "And is whatever is not wise ignorant?" she asked. "Do you not see that there is something in between wisdom and ignorance?" "And what might that be?" I said.

entries.before: '"Right opinion," she replied, "which, as you know, being incapable of giving a reason, is not knowledge (for how can knowledge be devoid of reason? Nor again, ignorance, for neither can ignorance attain the truth), but is clearly something which is a mean between ignorance and wisdom." "Quite true," I replied. "Do not then insist," she said, "that what is not fair is of necessity foul, or what is not good evil; or infer that because love is not fair and good he is therefore foul and evil — for he is in a mean between them." "Well," I said, "Love is surely admitted by all to be a great god." "By those who know or by those who do not know?" "By all." "And how, Socrates," she said with a smile, "can Love be acknowledged to be a great god by those who say that he is not a god at all?" "And who are they?" I said. "You and I are two of them," she replied. "How can that be?" I said. "It is quite intelligible," she replied, "for you yourself would acknowledge that the gods are happy and fair — of course you would — would you dare to say that any god was not?" "Certainly not," I replied. "And you mean by the happy, those who are the possessors of things good or fair?" "Yes." "And you admitted that Love, because he was in want, desires those good and fair things of which he is in want?" "Yes, I did." "But how can he be a god who has no portion in what is either good or fair?" "Impossible." "Then you see that you also deny the divinity of Love."'
entries.after: '"Right opinion," she replied. "As you know, right opinion means being right without being able to give a reason for it. So it is not knowledge, for how can there be knowledge without reason? Nor is it ignorance, for ignorance can never arrive at the truth. Clearly, then, it is something in between ignorance and wisdom." "Quite true," I replied. "Then do not insist," she said, "that whatever is not beautiful must be ugly, or that whatever is not good must be bad. And do not conclude that because love is not beautiful and good, he must therefore be ugly and bad; for he is in between them." "Well," I said, "surely Love is admitted by everyone to be a great god." "By those who know, or by those who do not know?" she asked. "By everyone." "And how, Socrates," she said with a smile, "can Love be admitted to be a great god by those who say that he is not a god at all?" "And who are they?" I said. "You and I are two of them," she replied. "How can that be?" I said. "It is easy to see," she replied, "for you yourself would admit that the gods are happy and beautiful — of course you would. Would you dare to say that any god was not?" "Certainly not," I replied. "And by the happy, you mean those who possess good or beautiful things?" "Yes." "And you admitted that Love, because he lacks good and beautiful things, desires the very things he lacks?" "Yes, I did." "But how can he be a god if he has no share in what is good or beautiful?" "Impossible." "Then you see that you too deny that Love is a god."
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: explain right opinion in plain sentences (being right without being able to give the reason, so neither knowledge nor ignorance); 'beautiful'/'ugly' for fair/foul throughout; 'in between'; 'has no share in'; keep every step of the argument that Socrates too denies Love is a god.
entries.renderer_notes: Right opinion is explained in plain sentences, with Jowett's two reasons (it cannot give a reason, so it is not knowledge; it reaches the truth, so it is not ignorance). Every step of the argument that Socrates too denies Love is a god is kept.

entries.before: '"What then is Love?" I asked. "Is he mortal?" "No." "What then?" "As in the former instance, he is neither mortal nor immortal, but in a mean between the two." "What is he, Diotima?" "He is a great spirit (daimon), and like all spirits he is intermediate between the divine and the mortal." "And what," I said, "is his power?" "He interprets," she replied, "between gods and men, conveying and taking across to the gods the prayers and sacrifices of men, and to men the commands and replies of the gods; he is the mediator who spans the chasm which divides them, and therefore in him all is bound together, and through him the arts of the prophet and the priest, their sacrifices and mysteries and charms, and all prophecy and incantation, find their way. For God mingles not with man; but through Love all the intercourse and converse of God with man, whether awake or asleep, is carried on. The wisdom which understands this is spiritual; all other wisdom, such as that of arts and handicrafts, is mean and vulgar. Now these spirits or intermediate powers are many and diverse, and one of them is Love." "And who," I said, "was his father, and who his mother?" "The tale," she said, "will take time; nevertheless I will tell you. On the birthday of Aphrodite there was a feast of the gods, at which the god Poros or Plenty, who is the son of Metis or Discretion, was one of the guests. When the feast was over, Penia or Poverty, as the manner is on such occasions, came about the doors to beg.'
entries.after: '"What then is Love?" I asked. "Is he mortal?" "No." "What then?" "As in the earlier case, he is neither mortal nor immortal, but in between the two." "What is he, Diotima?" "He is a great spirit, and like all spirits he is midway between the divine and the mortal." "And what," I said, "is his power?" "He interprets," she replied, "between gods and men. He carries the prayers and sacrifices of men across to the gods, and brings the commands and replies of the gods to men. He is the mediator who spans the gulf that divides them, and so in him everything is bound together. Through him the arts of the prophet and the priest find their way, with their sacrifices and mysteries and charms, and all prophecy and incantation. For a god does not mix with a human being; all communication and conversation between gods and men, whether men are awake or asleep, is carried on through Love. The wisdom which understands this is spiritual; all other wisdom, such as that of the arts and crafts, is lowly and workaday. Now these spirits, or in-between powers, are many and of many kinds, and one of them is Love." "And who," I said, "was his father, and who was his mother?" "The story," she said, "will take time; but I will tell you all the same. On Aphrodite's birthday the gods held a feast, and one of the guests was the god Poros, whose name means Plenty or Resource; he is the son of Metis, Cunning Intelligence. When the feast was over, Penia, or Poverty, came to the door to beg, as beggars do at a feast.

entries.before: 'Now Plenty who was the worse for nectar (there was no wine in those days) went into the garden of Zeus and fell into a heavy sleep; and Poverty, considering her own straitened circumstances, plotted to have a child by him, and accordingly she lay down at his side and conceived Love, who partly because he is naturally a lover of the beautiful, and because Aphrodite is herself beautiful, and also because he was born on her birthday, is her follower and attendant. And as his parentage is, so also are his fortunes. In the first place he is always poor, and anything but tender and fair, as the many imagine him; and he is rough and squalid, and has no shoes, nor a house to dwell in; on the bare earth exposed he lies under the open heaven, in the streets, or at the doors of houses, taking his rest; and like his mother he is always in distress. Like his father too, whom he also partly resembles, he is always plotting against the fair and good — he is bold, enterprising, strong, a mighty hunter, always weaving some intrigue or other, keen in the pursuit of wisdom, fertile in resources; a philosopher at all times, terrible as an enchanter, sorcerer, sophist. He is by nature neither mortal nor immortal, but alive and flourishing at one moment when he is in plenty, and dead at another moment, and again alive by reason of his father's nature.
entries.after: '"Now Plenty, who was drunk on nectar (there was no wine in those days), went into the garden of Zeus and fell into a heavy sleep. And Poverty, thinking of her own hard circumstances, plotted to have a child by him; so she lay down at his side and conceived Love. Love is Aphrodite's follower and attendant, partly because he is by nature a lover of the beautiful, and because Aphrodite is herself beautiful, and also because he was born on her birthday. His fortunes match his parentage. In the first place, he is always poor, and far from being tender and beautiful, as most people imagine him. He is rough and dirty, with no shoes and no house to live in. He sleeps on the bare ground, exposed under the open sky, in the streets or in doorways; and like his mother he is always in need. But he also partly resembles his father, and like him he is always scheming to win the beautiful and the good. He is bold, enterprising and strong, a mighty hunter, always weaving some intrigue or other, keen in the pursuit of wisdom, full of resources; a philosopher at all times, and formidable as an enchanter, a sorcerer and a sophist, one of those clever professional teachers of wisdom. By nature he is neither mortal nor immortal: at one moment, when he has plenty, he is alive and flourishing; at another he is dead; and then he comes alive again, because of his father's nature.

'Plotting against' becomes 'scheming to win', 'terrible' becomes 'formidable', and the sophist gloss is in line with R1's 'professional teachers' at 1.46. entries.before: But that which is always flowing in is always flowing out, and so he is never in want and never in wealth; and, further, he is in a mean between ignorance and knowledge. The truth of the matter is this: no god is a philosopher or seeker after wisdom, for he is wise already; nor does any man who is wise seek after wisdom. Neither do the ignorant seek after wisdom. For herein is the evil of ignorance, that he who is neither good nor wise is nevertheless satisfied with himself — he has no desire for that of which he feels no want." "But who then, Diotima," I said, "are the lovers of wisdom, if they are neither the wise nor the foolish?" "A child may answer that question," she replied. "They are those who are in a mean between the two; Love is one of them. For wisdom is a most beautiful thing, and Love is of the beautiful; and therefore Love is also a philosopher or lover of wisdom, and being a lover of wisdom is in a mean between the wise and the ignorant. And of this too his birth is the cause — for his father is wealthy and wise, and his mother poor and foolish. Such, my dear Socrates, is the nature of the spirit Love. The error in your conception of him was very natural, and as I imagine from what you say, has arisen out of a confusion of love and the beloved, which made you think that love was all beautiful. For the beloved is the truly beautiful, and delicate, and perfect, and blessed; but the principle of love is of another nature, and is such as I have described."'
entries.after: '"But whatever flows in to him is always flowing out again, and so he is never destitute and never rich; and he is also in between ignorance and knowledge. The truth of the matter is this: no god is a philosopher, a seeker after wisdom, for he is wise already; nor does any man who is wise seek after wisdom. Neither do the ignorant seek after wisdom. For this is what is bad about ignorance: someone who is neither good nor wise is nevertheless satisfied with himself, and he has no desire for what he does not feel he lacks." "But who, then, Diotima," I said, "are the lovers of wisdom, if they are neither the wise nor the foolish?" "A child could answer that question," she replied. "They are those who are in between the two, and Love is one of them. For wisdom is one of the most beautiful things, and Love is love of the beautiful; and so Love is also a philosopher, a lover of wisdom, and as a lover of wisdom he is in between the wise and the ignorant. His birth explains this too, for his father is rich and wise, and his mother poor and foolish. Such, my dear Socrates, is the nature of the spirit Love. Your mistaken idea of him was very natural. From what you say, I imagine it came from confusing love with the beloved — what loves with what is loved — and that made you think that love was entirely beautiful. For it is the beloved who is truly beautiful, and delicate, and perfect, and blessed; but what loves has a different nature, the one I have described."
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: 'in between'; 'this is what is bad about ignorance'; 'his birth explains this too'; make explicit that Socrates confused the lover, who lacks and longs, with the beloved, who is beautiful and blessed; keep the philosopher = lover of wisdom gloss.
entries.renderer_notes: 'What loves with what is loved' makes the confusion explicit without adding a claim; the description of what loves is left to what Diotima has just said. The current text had no opening quote here; both levels are now reopened.

entries.before: I said, '"O thou stranger woman, thou sayest well; but, assuming Love to be such as you say, what is the use of him to men?" "That, Socrates," she replied, "I will attempt to unfold. Of his nature and birth I have already spoken; and you acknowledge that love is of the beautiful. But some one will say: Of the beautiful in what, Socrates and Diotima? — or rather let me put the question more clearly, and ask: when a man loves the beautiful, what does he desire?" I answered her, "That the beautiful may be his." "Still," she said, "the answer suggests a further question: what is given by the possession of beauty?" "To what you have asked," I replied, "I have no answer ready." "Then," she said, "let me put the word good in the place of the beautiful, and repeat the question once more: if he who loves loves the good, what is it then that he loves?" "The possession of the good," I said. "And what does he gain who possesses the good?" "Happiness," I replied; "there is less difficulty in answering that question." "Yes," she said, "the happy are made happy by the acquisition of good things. Nor is there any need to ask why a man desires happiness; the answer is already final." "You are right," I said.'
entries.after: 'I said, "Well said, my friend from Mantineia. But if Love is as you say, what use is he to men?" "That, Socrates," she replied, "I will try to explain. I have already spoken of his nature and his birth, and you agree that love is love of the beautiful. But someone may ask us both, 'Socrates and Diotima, what is it about the beautiful that love wants?' Or rather, let me put the question more clearly: when a man loves the beautiful, what does he desire?" I answered her, "That the beautiful may be his." "Still," she said, "that answer raises a further question: what does possessing beauty give him?" "I have no answer ready for that question," I replied. "Then," she said, "let me put the word 'good' in place of the beautiful, and ask the question once more: if a man loves the good, what does he desire?" "The possession of the good," I said. "And what does someone who possesses the good gain?" "Happiness," I replied. "That question is easier to answer." "Yes," she said, "the happy are made happy by acquiring good things. And there is no need to ask why a man desires happiness; that answer is already final." "You are right," I said.
entries.assessor_fix: Light: a present-day address to Diotima as a visitor from abroad ('Well said...'; 'stranger' now means someone unknown); make the imagined question plain (what is it about beautiful things that love wants?); restore the marking of 'good' as a word (quotation marks lost in modernization); 'what does someone who has the good gain?'.
entries.renderer_notes: The current text had its opening quote after 'I said,'; Socrates' single quote now opens the paragraph. 'O thou stranger woman' becomes 'my friend from Mantineia': 'from Mantineia' keeps her status as a visitor from abroad, and 'my friend' is Socrates' polite address elsewhere ('Yes, my friend', 7.30). Both 'stranger' and a bare 'lady' would mislead or sound brusque today. The imagined question is left without inner quote marks, as in Jowett, and its wording is made plain. 'Good' is in single quotes as a third-level quotation, inside Diotima's double-quoted speech inside Socrates' single-quoted speech.

entries.before: '"And is this wish and this desire common to all? And do all men always desire their own good, or only some men? What say you?" "All men," I replied; "the desire is common to all." "Why, then," she rejoined, "are not all men, Socrates, said to love, but only some of them? Whereas you say that all men are always loving the same things." "I myself wonder," I said, "why this is." "There is nothing to wonder at," she replied, "the reason is that one part of love is separated off and receives the name of the whole, but the other parts have other names." "Give an illustration," I said. She answered me as follows: "There is poetry, which, as you know, is complex and manifold. All creation or passage of non-being into being is poetry or making, and the processes of all art are creative; and the masters of arts are all poets or makers." "Very true." "Still," she said, "you know that they are not called poets, but have other names; only that portion of the art which is separated off from the rest, and is concerned with music and metre, is termed poetry, and they who possess poetry in this sense of the word are called poets." "Very true," I said. "And the same holds of love.'
entries.after: '"And is this wish, this desire, common to all? Do all men always desire their own good, or only some men? What do you say?" "All men," I replied. "The desire is common to all." "Then why, Socrates," she asked, "do we not say that all men are in love, instead of saying that only some are? For you say that all men are always loving the same things." "I wonder about that myself," I said. "There is nothing to wonder at," she replied. "The reason is that one part of love is separated off and given the name of the whole, while the other parts have other names." "Give me an example," I said. She answered me as follows: "Take poetry, which, as you know, is complex and takes many forms. Our word for poetry literally means 'making': every act of creation, every passage from not-being into being, is poetry, or making. The processes of all the arts are creative, and so the masters of all the arts are poets, or makers." "Very true." "Still," she said, "you know that they are not called poets, but have other names. Only one part of the art, which is separated off from the rest and is concerned with music and meter, is called poetry; and only those who have poetry in this sense of the word are called poets." "Very true," I said. "And the same holds for love.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: add a few words that the Greek word for poetry literally means 'making', so every craftsman is strictly a 'poet' though the name is kept for verse-makers, which is the model for how 'love' is used; turn the 'Whereas' fragment into a full sentence; 'What do you say?'; 'those who'.
entries.renderer_notes: 'Our word for poetry literally means making' gives the Greek sense in Diotima's own voice, so the reader sees that every maker is strictly a 'poet' although the name is kept for verse-makers. The 'whereas' fragment becomes 'Yet you say ...'. Diotima's speech continues into 7.52, so neither quote is closed.

entries.before: 'For you may say generally that all desire of good and happiness is only the great and subtle power of love; but they who are drawn toward him by any other path, whether the path of money-making or gymnastics or philosophy, are not called lovers — the name of the whole is appropriated to those whose affection takes one form only; they alone are said to love, or to be lovers." "I dare say," I replied, "that you are right." "Yes," she added, "and you hear people say that lovers are seeking for their other half; but I say that they are seeking neither for the half of themselves, nor for the whole, unless the half or the whole be also a good. And they will cut off their own hands and feet and cast them away, if they are evil; for they love not what is their own, unless perchance there be some one who calls what belongs to him the good, and what belongs to another the evil. For there is nothing which men love but the good. Is there anything?" "Certainly, I should say, that there is nothing." "Then," she said, "the simple truth is, that men love the good." "Yes," I said. "To which must be added that they love the possession of the good?" "Yes, that must be added." "And not only the possession, but the everlasting possession of the good?" "That must be added too." "Then love," she said, "may be described generally as the love of the everlasting possession of the good?" "That is most true."'
entries.after: '"For you may say, in general, that every desire for good things and for happiness is simply the great and subtle power of love. But those who are drawn to him by some other path, whether the path of making money, or athletics, or philosophy, are not called lovers. Only those whose love takes one particular form, the love of one person for another, are given the name that belongs to the whole: they alone are said to love, or to be lovers." "You are probably right," I replied. "Yes," she added, "and you hear people say that lovers are seeking their other half. But I say that they are seeking neither the half of themselves nor the whole, unless that half or whole is also something good. And men will cut off their own hands and feet and throw them away, if they think those limbs are bad. For people do not love what is their own just because it is their own — unless perhaps someone calls whatever belongs to him good, and whatever belongs to another bad. entries.after: '"Then if this is the nature of love," she said, "can you tell me further how it is pursued? What are they doing, those who show all this eagerness and heat that is called love? entries.before: 'Beauty, then, is the destiny or goddess of parturition who presides at birth, and therefore, when approaching beauty, the conceiving power is propitious, and diffusive, and benign, and begets and bears fruit: at the sight of ugliness she frowns and contracts and has a sense of pain, and turns away, and shrivels up, and not without a pang refrains from conception. And this is the reason why, when the hour of conception arrives, and the teeming nature is full, there is such a flutter and ecstasy about beauty whose approach is the alleviation of the pain of travail. For love, Socrates, is not, as you imagine, the love of the beautiful only." "What then?" "The love of generation and of birth in beauty." "Yes," I said. "Yes, indeed," she replied. "But why of generation?" "Because to the mortal creature, generation is a sort of eternity and immortality," she replied; "and if, as has been already admitted, love is of the everlasting possession of the good, all men will necessarily desire immortality together with good: wherefore love is of immortality."'
entries.after: '"Beauty, then, is the goddess of destiny and of childbirth who presides over birth. So when a pregnant creature comes near beauty, it becomes gracious; it relaxes and opens; it is kindly, and it gives birth and bears fruit. But at the sight of ugliness it frowns and contracts and feels pain; it turns away and shrivels up, and, not without a pang, holds back from giving birth. That is why, when the time comes and the pregnant creature is full to bursting, there is such a flutter and ecstasy about beauty, because the approach of beauty relieves the pains of labor. For love, Socrates, is not, as you imagine, love of the beautiful only." "What then?" "The love of reproduction and of birth in beauty." "Yes," I said. "Yes, indeed," she replied. "But why is love the love of reproduction? Because for a mortal creature, reproduction is a kind of eternity and immortality. And if, as we have already agreed, love is the love of the everlasting possession of the good, then all men must necessarily desire immortality together with the good. entries.before: 'Nay, even in the life of the same individual there is succession and not absolute unity: a man is called the same, and yet in the short interval which elapses between youth and age, and in which every animal is said to have life and identity, he is undergoing a perpetual process of loss and reparation — hair, flesh, bones, blood, and the whole body are always changing. Which is true not only of the body, but also of the soul, whose habits, tempers, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, fears, never remain the same in any one of us, but are always coming and going; and equally true of knowledge, and what is still more surprising to us mortals, not only do the sciences in general spring up and decay, so that in respect of them we are never the same; but each of them individually experiences a like change. For what is implied in the word "recollection," but the departure of knowledge, which is ever being forgotten, and is renewed and preserved by recollection, and appears to be the same although in reality new, according to that law of succession by which all mortal things are preserved, not absolutely the same, but by substitution, the old worn-out mortality leaving another new and similar existence behind — unlike the divine, which is always the same and not another? And in this way, Socrates, the mortal body, or mortal anything, partakes of immortality; but the immortal in another way.'
entries.after: '"Indeed, even in the life of a single individual there is succession, not complete sameness. A man is called the same person; and yet in the short time between youth and old age, the time in which every living creature is said to be alive and to remain the same, he is going through a constant process of loss and renewal: his hair, flesh, bones, blood and whole body are always changing. And this is true not only of the body but also of the soul. Our habits, tempers, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains and fears never stay the same in any of us, but are always coming and going. It is equally true of knowledge; and, what is still more surprising to us mortals, not only do whole branches of knowledge spring up and decay in us, so that we are never the same with respect to them, but each single piece of knowledge undergoes the same change. For what does the word 'recollection' — calling knowledge back to mind — imply, if not that knowledge departs? Knowledge is always being forgotten, and it is renewed and preserved by recollection, so that it seems to be the same although in reality it is new. That is the law of succession by which all mortal things are preserved: not by remaining exactly the same, but by replacement, the old and worn-out mortal thing leaving behind another that is new and similar. The divine is different; it is always the same and never another. In this way, Socrates, the mortal body, or anything else mortal, shares in immortality; but what is immortal is immortal in another way.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast into shorter sentences: even one person's body, soul and knowledge are constantly lost and replaced; we need 'recollection' because knowledge leaves us and is replaced by new, similar knowledge; mortals share in immortality by such replacement, unlike the divine, which stays the same; 'loss and renewal'; 'branches of knowledge' for 'sciences'.

'Recollection' takes single quotes as a third-level quotation. 'Sciences' becomes 'branches of knowledge'. 'The immortal in another way' is completed as 'shares in it in another way'.

entries.before: He wanders about seeking beauty that he may beget offspring — for in deformity he will beget nothing — and naturally embraces the beautiful rather than the deformed body; above all when he finds a fair and noble and well-nurtured soul, he embraces the two in one person, and to such an one he is full of speech about virtue and the nature and pursuits of a good man; and he tries to educate him. entries.before: "These are the lesser mysteries of love, into which even you, Socrates, may enter; to the greater and more hidden ones which are the crown of these, and to which, if you pursue them in a right spirit, they will lead, I know not whether you will be able to attain. But I will do my utmost to inform you, and do you follow if you can. For he who would proceed aright in this matter should begin in youth to visit beautiful forms; and first, if he be guided by his instructor aright, to love one such form only — out of that he should create fair thoughts; and soon he will of himself perceive that the beauty of one form is akin to the beauty of another; and then, if beauty of form in general is his pursuit, how foolish would he be not to recognize that the beauty in every form is one and the same! And when he perceives this, he will abate his violent love of the one, which he will despise and deem a small thing, and will become a lover of all beautiful forms. In the next stage he will consider that the beauty of the mind is more honorable than the beauty of the outward form.
entries.after: '"These are the lesser mysteries of love, the first rites of initiation, into which even you, Socrates, may enter. Then there are the greater and more hidden mysteries, the final rites, which are the crown of these; and the lesser mysteries, if you pursue them in the right spirit, will lead you to them. Whether you will be able to attain to those, I do not know. But I will do my utmost to teach you, and you must follow if you can. For whoever would go about this matter rightly should begin in youth by turning to beautiful bodies. First, if the one who guides him through these mysteries leads him rightly, he should love one such body only, and out of that love he should create beautiful thoughts. Soon he will see for himself that the beauty of one body is akin to the beauty of another. And then, if beauty of body in general is what he pursues, how foolish he would be not to recognize that the beauty in all bodies is one and the same! When he sees this, he will relax his intense passion for the one, looking down on it and thinking it a small thing, and he will become a lover of all beautiful bodies. entries.before: "He who has been instructed thus far in the things of love, and who has learned to see the beautiful in due order and succession, when he comes toward the end will suddenly perceive a nature of wondrous beauty (and this, Socrates, is the final cause of all our former toils) — a nature which in the first place is everlasting, not growing and decaying, or waxing and waning; secondly, not fair in one point of view and foul in another, or at one time or in one relation or at one place fair, at another time or in another relation or at another place foul, as if fair to some and foul to others, or in the likeness of a face or hands or any other part of the bodily frame, or in any form of speech or knowledge, or existing in any other being, as for example, in an animal, or in heaven, or in earth, or in any other place; but beauty absolute, separate, simple, and everlasting, which without diminution and without increase, or any change, is imparted to the ever-growing and perishing beauties of all other things. He who from these ascending under the influence of true love begins to perceive that beauty, is not far from the end.
entries.after: '"Whoever has been instructed this far in the things of love, and has learned to see beautiful things in their proper order and succession, will, as he comes toward the end, suddenly perceive something wondrously beautiful in its nature — and this, Socrates, is the goal of all our earlier efforts. In the first place, it is everlasting: it does not grow and decay, or wax and wane. Secondly, it is not beautiful from one point of view and ugly from another; not beautiful at one time, or in one relation, or in one place, and ugly at another time, or in another relation, or in another place, as if it were beautiful to some and ugly to others. Nor does it take the likeness of a face or hands or any other part of the body; nor does it take the form of any speech or knowledge; nor does it exist in any other being, such as an animal, or the heavens, or the earth, or any other place. It is beauty itself, existing by itself and in itself, always one in form, and everlasting. Without growing less or greater, or changing in any way, it is shared by all the other beautiful things, which come into being and pass away. When someone rises from these through loving a young man in the right way and begins to perceive that beauty, he is not far from the end.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast keeping the whole cumulative list and its rhythm: 'beautiful'/'ugly' for fair/foul; repeat the negative so each item clearly says what this beauty is not (not a face, not a speech, not in any other thing); 'the goal of all our earlier efforts' for 'final cause'; un-invert the last sentence.
entries.renderer_notes: The cumulative list is kept, and 'nor' is repeated so that each item says what this beauty is not. The last sentence is un-inverted so that 'that beauty' cannot be read as the start of a that-clause.

entries.before: And the true order of going, or being led by another, to the things of love, is to begin from the beauties of earth and mount upwards for the sake of that other beauty, using these as steps only, and from one going on to two, and from two to all fair forms, and from fair forms to fair practices, and from fair practices to fair notions, until from fair notions he arrives at the notion of absolute beauty, and at last knows what the essence of beauty is. entries.after: '"And the true order of going, or of being led by another, to the things of love is this: to begin from the beauties of earth and climb upward for the sake of that other beauty, using these only as steps — from one beautiful body to two, and from two to all beautiful bodies; from beautiful bodies to beautiful institutions, and from beautiful institutions to beautiful branches of knowledge; until from these he arrives at the knowledge of absolute beauty, and at last knows what the essence of beauty is. This, my dear Socrates," said the woman from Mantineia, "is the life above all others that a man should live, in the contemplation of absolute beauty. If you once saw that beauty, you would see that it is not to be measured against gold, and fine clothes, and beautiful boys and young men, whose presence now entrances you. You and many others would be content to live just seeing them and talking with them, without food or drink, if that were possible — you want only to look at them and to be with them. But what if a man had eyes to see the true beauty — the divine beauty, I mean, pure and clear and unmixed, not clogged with the pollutions of mortality and all the colors and empty trifles of human life? entries.after: When Socrates had finished speaking, the company applauded. Aristophanes was starting to say something in answer to the allusion Socrates had made to his own speech, the one about lovers seeking their other half, when suddenly there was a loud knocking at the door of the house, as if a party of revelers had arrived, and the sound of a flute-girl could be heard. Agathon told the attendants to go and see who the intruders were. 'If they are friends of ours,' he said, 'invite them in; but if not, say that the drinking is over.' A little while later they heard the voice of Alcibiades, the famous Athenian politician and general, ringing through the courtyard. He was very drunk, and kept roaring and shouting, 'Where is Agathon? Take me to Agathon!' At last, propped up by the flute-girl and some of his attendants, he found his way to them. 'Greetings, friends,' he said, appearing at the door crowned with a massive garland of ivy and violets, with ribbons streaming from his head. 'Will you have a very drunk man as a companion in your revels? Or shall I just crown Agathon, which is what I came to do, and go away? I couldn't come yesterday, and that is why I am here today, with these ribbons on my head: I mean to take them off my own head and crown the head of the most beautiful and wisest of men — if I may be allowed to call him that. Will you laugh at me because I'm drunk? Laugh if you like; I know very well that I am speaking the truth. But first tell me: if I come in, will you accept the terms I mentioned, and take me in as drunk as I am?

entries.before: 'And now, my boys, I shall praise Socrates in a figure which will appear to him to be a caricature, and yet I speak, not to make fun of him, but only for the truth's sake. I say, that he is exactly like the busts of Silenus, which are set up in the statuaries' shops, holding pipes and flutes in their mouths; and they are made to open in the middle, and have images of gods inside them. I say also that he is like Marsyas the satyr. You yourself will not deny, Socrates, that your face is like that of a satyr. Aye, and there is a resemblance in other points too. For example, you are a bully, as I can prove by witnesses, if you will not confess. And are you not a flute-player? That you are, and a performer far more wonderful than Marsyas. He indeed with instruments used to charm the souls of men by the power of his breath, and the players of his music do so still — for the melodies of Olympus are derived from Marsyas who taught them, and these, whether they are played by a great master or by a miserable flute-girl, have a power which no others have; they alone possess the soul and reveal the wants of those who have need of gods and mysteries, because they are divine. But you produce the same effect with your words only, and do not require the flute — that is the difference between you and him.
entries.after: 'And now, my friends, I shall praise Socrates by means of an image, which he will take for a caricature; but I am not using it to make fun of him, only for the sake of the truth. I say that he is exactly like the busts of Silenus, the pot-bellied old satyr, that you see set up in the sculptors' shops, holding pipes and flutes in their mouths. They are hollow and made to open down the middle, and inside them are images of gods. I say also that he is like Marsyas the satyr, the legendary flute-player. You yourself won't deny, Socrates, that your face looks like a satyr's. Yes, and you resemble them in other ways too. For example, you are insolent, as I can prove with witnesses, if you won't confess it. And aren't you a flute-player? You certainly are, and a far more wonderful performer than Marsyas. He, it is true, used instruments to charm people's souls with the power of his breath, and anyone who plays his music still does so today. For the melodies of the musician Olympus, Marsyas's pupil, come from Marsyas, who taught them to him; and these melodies, whether a great master plays them or a second-rate flute-girl, have a power that no others have. They alone take possession of the soul, and they reveal which listeners are in need of the gods and their secret rites, because the melodies themselves are divine. But you produce the same effect with words alone, without needing a flute. That is the difference between you and him.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: 'by means of an image'; a few words on the Silenus figures (hollow statuettes of the pot-bellied old satyr, sold in sculptors' shops, that open to show gods inside); 'insolent' or 'outrageous' for 'bully' (today someone who intimidates the weak); 'Olympus, Marsyas's pupil' (not the mountain); say plainly that these tunes seize listeners and reveal who needs the gods and their rites; 'Yes' for 'Aye'.

entries.before: When we hear any other speaker, even a very good one, he produces absolutely no effect upon us, or not much, whereas the mere fragments of you and your words, even at second-hand, and however imperfectly repeated, amaze and possess the souls of every man, woman, and child who comes within hearing of them. And if I were not afraid that you would think me hopelessly drunk, I would have sworn as well as spoken to the influence which they have always had and still have over me. For my heart leaps within me more than that of any Corybantian reveller, and my eyes rain tears when I hear them. And I observe that many others are affected in the same manner. I have heard Pericles and other great orators, and I thought that they spoke well, but I never had any similar feeling; my soul was not stirred by them, nor was I angry at the thought of my own slavish state. But this Marsyas has often brought me to such a pass, that I have felt as if I could hardly endure the life which I am leading (this, Socrates, you will admit); and I am conscious that if I did not shut my ears against him, and fly as from the voice of the siren, my fate would be like that of others — he would transfix me, and I should grow old sitting at his feet. For he makes me confess that I ought not to live as I do, neglecting the wants of my own soul, and busying myself with the concerns of the Athenians; therefore I hold my ears and tear myself away from him.
entries.after: 'When we hear any other speaker, even a very good one, he has absolutely no effect on us, or not much; but mere fragments of you and your words, even at second hand, and however badly repeated, amaze and possess the souls of every man, woman, and child who hears them. And if I weren't afraid you would think me hopelessly drunk, I would swear on oath, and not just tell you, what an effect your words have always had on me, and still have. For when I hear them, my heart leaps inside me even more than the hearts of the Corybantian revelers — those worshipers who dance in a religious frenzy — and my eyes rain tears. And I see that many others are affected in the same way. I have heard the statesman Pericles and other great orators, and I thought they spoke well, but I never felt anything like this; my soul was not stirred by them, nor was I angry at the thought of my own slavish state. But this Marsyas here has often driven me to the point where I felt I could hardly bear to go on living the life I lead — this, Socrates, you will admit. And I know that if I did not stop my ears against him and flee, as from the Sirens' song, the same thing would happen to me as to others: he would hold me transfixed, and I would grow old sitting at his feet. For he makes me confess that I ought not to live as I do, neglecting the needs of my own soul and busying myself with the affairs of the Athenians. So I hold my ears and tear myself away from him.

entries.before: And this is what I and many others have suffered from the flute-playing of this satyr. Yet hear me once more while I show you how exact the image is, and how marvellous his power. For let me tell you — none of you know him; but I will reveal him to you, having begun, I must go on. See you how fond he is of the fair? He is always with them and is always being smitten by them, and then again he knows nothing and is ignorant of all things — such is the appearance which he puts on. Is he not like a Silenus in this? To be sure he is: his outer mask is the carved head of the Silenus; but, O my companions in drink, when he is opened, what temperance there is residing within! Know you that beauty and wealth and honor, at which the many wonder, are of no account with him, and are utterly despised by him — he regards not at all the persons who are gifted with them; mankind are nothing to him; all his life is spent in mocking and flouting at them. But when I opened him, and looked within at his serious purpose, I saw in him divine and golden images of such fascinating beauty that I was ready to do in a moment whatever Socrates commanded; they may have escaped the observation of others, but I saw them. Now I fancied that he was seriously enamored of my beauty, and I thought that I should therefore have a grand opportunity of hearing him tell what he knew, for I had a wonderful opinion of the attractions of my youth.
entries.after: 'And this is what I and many others have suffered from the flute-playing of this satyr. But hear me once more, while I show you how exact the image is, and how marvelous his power. For let me tell you, none of you knows him; but I will reveal him to you. Having begun, I must go on. Do you see how he is drawn to beautiful young men? He is always around them, always being smitten by them; and then again, he knows nothing and is ignorant of everything. That is the appearance he puts on. Isn't he like a Silenus in this? Of course he is. His outer mask is the carved head of the Silenus; but, my fellow drinkers, when he is opened up, what self-control you find inside! Believe me, beauty and wealth and honor, which most people marvel at, count for nothing with him; he utterly despises them. He does not care at all about the people who have them; human beings are nothing to him; he spends his whole life mocking and scorning them. But when I opened him up and looked inside at his serious purpose, I saw in him divine and golden images of such fascinating beauty that I was ready to do in a moment whatever Socrates commanded. Others may not have noticed them, but I saw them. Now, I imagined that he was seriously in love with my beauty, and I thought this would give me a grand opportunity to hear him tell me everything he knew; for I had a wonderfully high opinion of my youthful charms.
entries.assessor_fix: Light: restore a full stop before 'having begun' (the modern comma creates a run-on); 'Do you see how he is drawn to beautiful young men?'; 'self-control' for 'temperance' (at a drinking party it reads as abstinence); 'Believe me'; 'he does not care at all about'; 'mocking and scorning'.

entries.before: In the prosecution of this design, when I next went to him, I sent away the attendant who usually accompanied me (I will confess the whole truth, and beg you to listen; and if I speak falsely, do you, Socrates, expose the falsehood). Well, he and I were alone together, and I thought that when there was nobody with us, I should hear him speak the language which lovers use to their loves when they are by themselves, and I was delighted. Nothing of the sort; he conversed as usual, and spent the day with me and then went away. Afterwards I challenged him to the palaestra, and he wrestled and closed with me several times when there was no one present; I fancied that I might succeed in this manner. Not a bit — I made no way with him. Lastly, as I had failed hitherto, I thought that I must take stronger measures and attack him boldly, and, as I had begun, not give him up, but see how matters stood between him and me. So I invited him to sup with me, just as if he were a fair youth, and I a designing lover. He was not easily persuaded to come; he did, however, after a while accept the invitation, and when he came the first time, he wanted to go away at once as soon as supper was over, and I had not the face to detain him. The second time, still in pursuance of my design, after we had supped, I went on conversing far into the night, and when he wanted to go away, I pretended that the hour was late and that he had much better remain.
entries.after: 'To carry out this plan, the next time I went to see him I sent away the attendant who usually came with me. I will confess the whole truth, and I beg you to listen; and if I say anything false, you, Socrates, must expose it. Well, he and I were alone together, and I thought that now, with nobody else there, I would hear him speak to me the way a lover speaks to his beloved when they are alone, and I was delighted. Nothing of the sort. He talked with me as usual, spent the day with me, and then went away. Next I challenged him to a match at the wrestling school, and he wrestled and grappled with me several times with no one else there; I imagined I might get somewhere that way. Not a bit of it; I got nowhere with him. Finally, since I had failed so far, I thought I must take stronger measures and go after him boldly: since I had started, I would not give up on him, but would find out how matters stood between him and me. So I invited him to dinner, just as if our roles were reversed and he were the beautiful youth and I the older lover with designs on him. He was not easily persuaded to come, but after a while he did accept the invitation. The first time he came, he wanted to leave as soon as dinner was over, and I didn't have the nerve to keep him. The second time, still following my plan, I went on talking with him after dinner far into the night, and when he wanted to go, I made the excuse that it was late and that he had much better stay.

entries.before: So he lay down on the couch next to me, the same on which he had supped, and there was no one but ourselves sleeping in the apartment. All this may be told without shame to anyone. But what follows I could hardly tell you if I were sober. Yet as the proverb says, 'in vino veritas,' whether with boys, or without them; and therefore I must speak. Nor, again, should I be justified in concealing the lofty actions of Socrates when I come to praise him. Moreover I have felt the serpent's sting; and he who has suffered, as they say, is willing to tell his fellow-sufferers only, as they alone will be likely to understand him, and will not be extreme in judging of the sayings or doings which have been wrung from his agony. For I have been bitten by a more than viper's tooth; I have known in my soul, or in my heart, or in some other part, that worst of pangs, more violent in ingenuous youth than any serpent's tooth, the pang of philosophy, which will make a man say or do anything. And you whom I see around me, Phaedrus and Agathon and Eryximachus and Pausanias and Aristodemus and Aristophanes — all of you, and I need not say Socrates himself — have had experience of the same madness and passion in your longing after wisdom. Therefore listen and excuse my doings then and my sayings now. But let the attendants and other profane and unmannered persons close up the doors of their ears.
entries.after: 'So he lay down on the couch next to me, the same couch he had reclined on at dinner, and no one but the two of us was sleeping in the room. All this could be told to anyone without shame. But what comes next I could hardly tell you if I were sober. Still, as the proverb says, "In vino veritas": in wine there is truth. Another saying has it that wine and children both tell the truth; so wine tells the truth with children or without them, and therefore I must speak. Nor, again, would it be right for me to hide the lofty conduct of Socrates when I have set out to praise him. What's more, I have felt the serpent's bite; and a man who has been bitten, as they say, is willing to talk about it only to his fellow sufferers, because they alone are likely to understand him, and will not judge too harshly the things his agony drove him to say or do. For I have been bitten by something worse than a viper. In my soul, or in my heart, or in some other part of me, I have known the worst pang of all, which bites a gifted young mind more painfully than any serpent's tooth: the pang of philosophy, which will make a man say or do anything. And all of you I see around me — Phaedrus and Agathon and Eryximachus and Pausanias and Aristodemus and Aristophanes, and I need not mention Socrates himself — all of you have experienced the same madness and passion in your longing for wisdom. So listen, and forgive what I did then and what I am saying now. But, as at the sacred mysteries, let the attendants and anyone else who is uninitiated or ill-mannered close up the doors of their ears.
entries.assessor_fix: Recast: 'room' for 'apartment'; spell out the proverb (wine, with or without children, both said to tell the truth); 'more painful to a gifted young mind' ('ingenuous' now means naive); 'the uninitiated' for 'profane', as at the mysteries; 'dined'; keep the snakebite image and the list of those present.
entries.renderer_notes: The double proverb is spelled out: 'in vino veritas' plus 'wine and children tell the truth'. It uses 'children', not Jowett's 'boys', because in this passage 'boys' would read as lovers. The proverb is a quotation inside speech, so it takes double quotes.

entries.before: When the lamp was put out and the servants had gone away, I thought that I must be plain with him and have no more ambiguity. So I gave him a shake, and I said: 'Socrates, are you asleep?' 'No,' he said. 'Do you know what I am meditating?' 'What are you meditating?' he said. 'I think,' I replied, 'that of all the lovers whom I have ever had you are the only one who is worthy of me, and you appear to be too modest to speak. Now I feel that I should be a fool to refuse you this or any other favor, and therefore I come to lay at your feet all that I have and all that my friends have, in the hope that you will assist me in the way of virtue, which I desire above all things, and in which I believe that you can help me better than anyone else. And I should certainly have more reason to be ashamed of what wise men would say if I were to refuse a favor to such as you, than of what the world, who are mostly fools, would say of me if I granted it.' To these words he replied in the ironical manner which is so characteristic of him: 'Alcibiades, my friend, you have indeed an elevated aim if what you say is true, and if there really is in me any power by which you may become better — truly you must see in me some rare beauty of a kind infinitely higher than any which I see in you. And therefore, if you mean to share with me and to exchange beauty for beauty, you will have greatly the advantage of me; you will gain true beauty in return for appearance — like Diomede, gold in exchange for brass.

entries.before: Agathon was getting up to take a place on the couch beside Socrates when suddenly a crowd of revelers burst in, throwing the whole party into confusion. Someone leaving had left the front door open, and they poured in without ceremony. The noise was tremendous, all order vanished, and everyone was forced to drink enormous quantities of wine. Aristodemus said that Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and some others left at that point, while he himself fell asleep and slept for a long time — the nights were long at that season. He woke near dawn, as the cocks were crowing, and saw that most of the company were either asleep or had gone. Only Agathon, Aristophanes, and Socrates were still awake, drinking from a large bowl that they passed around from left to right. Socrates was arguing with them. Aristodemus couldn't remember most of what was said — he'd missed the beginning and was still half asleep — but the gist was that Socrates was forcing them to admit that the same person could be skilled at writing both comedy and tragedy, and that a true master of tragedy must also be a master of comedy. They were being compelled to agree, though they weren't entirely following the argument and kept nodding off. Aristophanes fell asleep first, and then, as daylight was breaking, Agathon. Socrates, having put them both to sleep, got up and left. Aristodemus followed him, as was his habit. Socrates went to the Lyceum, bathed, and spent the rest of the day as usual. In the evening, he went home to bed.

Socrates, having put them both to sleep, got up and left. Aristodemus followed him, as was his habit. Socrates went to the Lyceum, bathed, and spent the rest of the day as usual. In the evening, he went home to bed.
